evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Catadromous species occupying Atlantic coastal rivers, estuaries and accessible inland waters.
evidence.observedEffect: Confirms Mid-Atlantic presence and intentional baited-hook/trap fisheries, with major life-stage differences.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Distribution, life history and fishery relevance
evidence.limitations: Agency account does not establish numerical bite rules.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Daytime observations during mass movement of amphidromous prey in a tropical stream.
evidence.observedEffect: American eels fed diurnally when concentrated migrating prey were available.
evidence.limitations: Tropical prey pulse and river setting are exceptional; not a daytime bonus for NOVA.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Upper Delaware River stomach samples.
evidence.observedEffect: Macroinvertebrates dominated many feeding eels; prey composition changed with fish size and local availability.
evidence.limitations: No environmental catchability response was isolated.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Acoustic/ultrasonic telemetry in tidal creeks and estuary.
evidence.observedEffect: Eels showed diel and tidal movement cycles tied to habitat use.
evidence.limitations: Movement is not feeding; baited-capture evidence should control scoring.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Telemetry/activity observations across tidal stages.
evidence.observedEffect: Tides influenced movement and daily activity cycle.
evidence.limitations: No direct feeding or hook-and-line endpoint; no tide bonus.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Silver-stage downstream migration and digestive regression described in authoritative life history.
evidence.observedEffect: Migrating silver eels reduce or cease feeding as they prepare for oceanic spawning migration.
evidence.novaApplicability: mechanistically important but life stage usually unavailable to app
evidence.limitations: Do not infer silver stage from season alone; target fisheries and regulations differ.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Searches for pressure, fronts, moon, wind and ordinary rainfall effects on feeding/catchability.
evidence.observedEffect: Movement studies included hydrologic or lunar covariates, but no qualifying direct feeding or hook-and-line rule survived.
evidence.limitations: Rain/discharge can alter access and migration without increasing appetite.

evidence.variable: time of day and baited capture
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Eight baited eel traps checked every 3 h for six 24-h periods in early September; 322 captures.
evidence.observedEffect: 178 eels (55%) were captured just after sunset at the 20:00 check, 140 (44%) during the remainder of night, and only 4 (1%) in daylight.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Baited-trap capture as contemporaneous foraging proxy
evidence.lifeStage: mostly yellow eel, mean about 31 cm
evidence.novaApplicability: strong direct endpoint for estuarine late-summer/fall conditions
evidence.limitations: Baited traps are not hook-and-line; salinity, turbidity, season and bait odor limit transfer.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Traps checked every 30 min from 17:15-20:15 for six evenings in early October; 588 captures.
evidence.observedEffect: First captures consistently occurred just after sunset, peaked about one hour after sunset, then declined.
evidence.novaApplicability: strong timing evidence within study season
evidence.limitations: Not a universal civil-clock window; sunset, season and estuary conditions define the observation.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Eels acclimated between 10 and 20 C versus winter temperatures at or below 5 C for more than five weeks.
evidence.observedEffect: Eels at 10-20 C fed regularly; those acclimated to winter-cold conditions ceased feeding and entered profound metabolic torpor.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Observed feeding state and oxygen consumption
evidence.novaApplicability: direct feeding evidence with chronic-exposure limitation
evidence.limitations: Does not support a rapid penalty from a one-day cold front or an exact field cutoff across populations.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Maryland eels acclimated to 6, 12, 18, 24 and 30 C, then tested in a gradient.
evidence.observedEffect: Final preferendum was about 16.7 C and selected temperature was not strongly shifted by acclimation.
evidence.limitations: Thermal preference is not maximum feeding or catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Trawl sampling in brackish portions of three Virginia rivers.
evidence.observedEffect: Fewer eels were caught during colder months; abundance in trawl surveys was related to water temperature.
evidence.novaApplicability: high regional relevance, but abundance/catchability confounded
evidence.limitations: Trawl catch can reflect movement, depth and abundance; no per-fish feeding coefficient.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Brackish Virginia rivers.
evidence.observedEffect: Polychaetes, crustaceans and bivalves were important prey, including soft-shell clams and blue crabs.
evidence.limitations: Diet composition does not quantify feeding rate.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Radio-tagged 518-810 mm yellow eels near Millville Dam.
evidence.observedEffect: Seasonal movement and upstream activity covaried with temperature and discharge.
evidence.limitations: Movement is not feeding or hook vulnerability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Long-term telemetry and hoop-net records; activity decreased at low temperature.
evidence.observedEffect: Activity declined around 8 C and ceased near 4 C; greatest seasonal activity/hoop-net catch occurred around 8.1-11.1 C in the study system.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Movement distance, depth and commercial hoop-net catch
evidence.limitations: Hoop-net catch combines activity, gear encounter and seasonal aggregation; do not merge with lab feeding into a smooth curve.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Accepted as Pomoxis nigromaculatus; supplied and accepted names match.
evidence.observedEffect: No species-level name change affecting Northern Virginia was identified.
evidence.novaApplicability: Direct naming applicability; not a score input
evidence.limitations: Taxonomic identity does not imply behavioral uniformity among populations.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Black crappie sampled in Lake Opinicon across sizes and seasons.
evidence.observedEffect: Diet shifted progressively with size and available prey; the species used planktonic and larger prey as it grew.
evidence.limitations: Diet composition does not provide a bite-score multiplier and full text was not accessible in this review.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Field observations of several Great Lakes-region fishes at low seasonal temperatures.
evidence.observedEffect: Black crappie were among species reported feeding at low temperatures; no universal cessation temperature was established for adult angling.
evidence.evidenceType: field feeding study cited in authoritative synopsis
evidence.novaApplicability: Relevant only as evidence against a hard folklore cessation threshold
evidence.limitations: The underlying older article was not available in full text here; exact population, sizes, and temperatures should be rechecked before calibration.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Spring to early-summer nesting; males build and guard nests.
evidence.observedEffect: Reproductive behavior can aggregate fish and produce defensive responses, but no direct black-crappie angling study isolated feeding from nest defense.
evidence.limitations: Spawning temperature and calendar values are not converted into bite optima.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Barometric pressure, fronts, wind, ordinary rain, cloud cover, and moon phase.
evidence.observedEffect: No qualifying black-crappie study directly isolated these variables for feeding, foraging, or hook-and-line catchability.
evidence.limitations: Absence of evidence is not proof of no biological effect; it is sufficient to reject unsupported production weight.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Recent angling exposure independent of harvest and abundance.
evidence.observedEffect: No qualifying black-crappie experiment separated learning or hook avoidance from depletion, size selectivity, effort, or fish density.
evidence.novaApplicability: Directly relevant to withholding a pressure rule
evidence.limitations: Tag-return studies show selectivity but do not isolate learning.

evidence.variable: Regional occurrence, habitat, diet, and recreational use
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Virginia ponds, lakes, reservoirs, and slow river habitats.
evidence.observedEffect: Black crappie are an established Virginia sport fish associated with cover and open-water prey; the account supports targetability and regional context.
evidence.novaApplicability: High regional relevance; not a per-fish bite function
evidence.limitations: The page does not isolate short-term feeding or catchability from abundance and access.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Tagged fish 20.0–39.8 cm total length; angler returns 20.0–38.8 cm; five southern reservoirs.
evidence.observedEffect: Return probability was low near 20 cm, highest approximately 26–32 cm, and declined among longer fish.
evidence.novaApplicability: Direct catchability evidence, but transfer is limited by gear, regulations, fish size structure, and region
evidence.limitations: The relationship is not a universal smooth curve and should be bounded to the measured size range.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Spring and fall 1992–1993; black, white, and natural hybrid crappies in Weiss Reservoir.
evidence.observedEffect: Black crappies were overrepresented in angler catch relative to independent sampling, while white crappies were underrepresented.
evidence.novaApplicability: Supports population/species context, not a real-time environmental multiplier
evidence.limitations: The study was one reservoir and phenotype composition, gear, abundance, and hybrid identification may limit transfer.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 0, 25, and 50 NTU controlled treatments.
evidence.observedEffect: Juvenile black crappies maintained foraging and consumed greater diet biomass than white crappies; the tested turbidity range did not cause a general feeding collapse.
evidence.novaApplicability: Useful to reject a generic 0–50 NTU penalty for juveniles; not an adult angling threshold
evidence.limitations: Juvenile, controlled conditions and live invertebrate prey do not directly represent adult lure catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 0, 25, and 50 NTU with Chaoborus, Chironomus, Daphnia, and other prey.
evidence.observedEffect: Black crappies showed stronger prey-size selectivity; Chaoborus were preferred, Chironomus avoided, and Daphnia avoided by black crappies.
evidence.limitations: Prey assemblage and juvenile size are highly specific.

evidence.variable: Winter dissolved oxygen, temperature, and current
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Backwater conditions with dissolved oxygen above or below 2 mg/L, temperature around/below 1°C, and current around/above 1 cm/s.
evidence.observedEffect: When dissolved oxygen exceeded 2 mg/L, black crappies selected water above 1°C and little detectable current; below 2 mg/L they moved toward higher oxygen even when colder or flowing.
evidence.lifeStage: Mixed sizes in winter field telemetry/sampling
evidence.novaApplicability: Winter location context; not feeding or catchability
evidence.limitations: The endpoint was habitat selection, not prey consumption or angling. Exact thresholds are season- and system-specific.

evidence.variable: Adult movement and seasonal space use
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Ultrasonic telemetry April–August 1991.
evidence.observedEffect: Adult black crappie movement and habitat use changed through spring and summer in Brant Lake.
evidence.limitations: Movement is not a feeding-rate measurement and the lake differs from Northern Virginia reservoirs and rivers.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: May and July sampling across 1.5–7.0 m depth zones.
evidence.observedEffect: Black crappies showed a distinct July diel movement, largely absent from the study area by day and returning at night to feed.
evidence.novaApplicability: Supports context-dependent nocturnal feeding in one lake, not a universal night bonus
evidence.limitations: Only an abstract/synopsis was accessible; results are assemblage- and season-specific.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Summer sampling, Lake Ontario tributary
evidence.observedEffect: Blacknose dace fed most heavily during crepuscular periods, with a main peak from 1600-2000 h and a smaller peak from 0400-0800 h.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Stomach fullness/diet through the diel cycle
evidence.limitations: Single tributary and summer season; original full article was not independently inspected, so the rule must remain conditional rather than universal.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 20 C acclimation; 16L:8D versus 8L:16D
evidence.observedEffect: Long-day fish had incipient upper lethal temperature 29.9 C versus 28.8 C under short days, and generally longer resistance times.
evidence.limitations: Survival and lethal tolerance are not feeding optima; do not use these values as bite thresholds.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Susquehanna River tributary stock
evidence.observedEffect: Embryo-to-juvenile development was described for blacknose and longnose dace.
evidence.limitations: Early-life development does not support adult feeding or catchability rules.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Broad targeted search
evidence.observedEffect: No qualifying intentional hook-and-line fishery or catchability experiment was located; the species is small and normally functions as a forage/minnow species.
evidence.limitations: Microfishing can intentionally target dace, but production BiteMap prioritization is weak.

evidence.variable: dissolved oxygen, turbidity, pressure, fronts, moon, stocking, angling pressure
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Broad variable-specific searches
evidence.observedEffect: No direct species-specific feeding or catchability response adequate for scoring was found.
evidence.limitations: Absence of evidence is not evidence of no biological effect.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: June through September
evidence.observedEffect: Chironomid larvae were the major prey, but their contribution generally declined from June to September.
evidence.limitations: Changing diet share may reflect prey phenology and does not quantify total feeding rate.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Diel samples in Trucka Brook
evidence.observedEffect: Blacknose dace diets were closely associated with benthic prey; a mayfly nymph was a major prey item in the fish community.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Fish diets compared with benthos and drift
evidence.limitations: Multi-species study; no portable blacknose-dace effect size for a BiteMap score was extracted.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Late November as water temperature declined below 5.0 C
evidence.observedEffect: Dace moved into crevices beneath rubble; mean maximum rubble diameter was 15.9 cm.
evidence.limitations: Habitat occupancy and movement were measured, not feeding or catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Winter versus summer observations
evidence.observedEffect: Winter focal depth was greater and mid-depth water velocity was faster than in summer.
evidence.limitations: Location context only; cannot infer a winter bite increase or decrease.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Populations from streams with different current velocities
evidence.observedEffect: Swimming performance mirrored home-stream current velocity.
evidence.limitations: Performance adaptation is not feeding rate, and population effects limit transfer.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Populations across an urbanization gradient
evidence.observedEffect: Performance differences showed environmental correlates, plasticity, and repeatability among populations.
evidence.limitations: Population performance does not directly predict feeding or hook-and-line catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Eastern half of North America
evidence.observedEffect: Large genetic differences support separation of eastern R. atratulus and western R. obtusus; R. atratulus occurs east of the Appalachians from Nova Scotia to Virginia and in part of the eastern Great Lakes.
evidence.limitations: Older western blacknose-dace studies may involve R. obtusus or a broad species concept and must not be transferred silently to NOVA.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Juvenile dace exposed to varying creek-chub density and habitat structure
evidence.observedEffect: When structure at predator locations was low, dace avoided predators at night but not during the day; response did not scale with predator density in that treatment.
evidence.limitations: Predation avoidance is not feeding; juvenile artificial-stream behavior should not become an angling rule.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Virginia and Maryland agency accounts identify established blue-catfish fisheries and intentional hook-and-line targeting.
evidence.observedEffect: Confirms practical, intentional regional targeting.
evidence.limitations: Agency guidance does not validate weather or feeding thresholds.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Reward-tag study beginning at 381 mm TL in Missouri and Mississippi river reaches.
evidence.observedEffect: Recreational blue-catfish exploitation was highest at 840-890 mm in the Missouri River (0.34-0.43) and 891-1,015 mm in the Mississippi River (0.24-0.28).
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Size-specific reported harvest/catch-and-release corrected for reporting
evidence.novaApplicability: direct catchability/exploitation endpoint but low geographic portability
evidence.limitations: Exploitation includes angler selectivity, abundance, regulations, gear and harvest decisions; not an intrinsic smooth size curve.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Stratified sampling across a Chesapeake Bay subestuary.
evidence.observedEffect: Large numbers occupied tidal freshwater and oligohaline habitats, with abundance patterns tied to habitat and season.
evidence.limitations: Occupancy and electrofishing abundance do not establish feeding or hook-and-line catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Two annual telemetry cycles in a 97-km lower Missouri River reach.
evidence.observedEffect: Intra-annual movement and tributary use varied; tributary use during putative spawning was 10% in 2006 and 18% in 2007, and a May 2007 flood was a possible contributor.
evidence.limitations: Movement/spawning access is not feeding; flood attribution was not isolated experimentally.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Spring sampling of nonnative catfish and migrating alosines in the James River.
evidence.observedEffect: Catfish consumed alosines, but prey use depended on species, predator size, prey availability and season.
evidence.limitations: Seasonal prey occurrence cannot be converted into a general spring bite bonus.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Broad search for species-specific direct feeding or hook-and-line experiments isolating pressure, fronts, wind, moon or cloud cover.
evidence.observedEffect: No qualifying direct evidence was verified.
evidence.limitations: Absence of verified evidence is not proof of no biological effect; it supports zero model weight.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Laboratory trials at 5, 15, and 25 C; fish 332-878 mm TL; salinity near 3.0 per mille; 14-day acclimation; 72-hour pretrial starvation.
evidence.observedEffect: Mean maximum 24-hour consumption increased from 7.53% body weight at 5 C to 10.66% at 15 C; 15 and 25 C did not differ significantly (25 C mean 10.55%).
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Maximum daily ration (% body weight per 24 h)
evidence.populationLocation: Laboratory fish associated with Virginia tidal-river research
evidence.novaApplicability: mechanistically relevant; exact laboratory conditions must be preserved
evidence.limitations: Maximum-ration, starved-fish laboratory result is not a natural catch-rate curve; only three temperatures were tested.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Gizzard shad versus blue crab in 24-hour laboratory feeding trials at tested temperatures and fish sizes.
evidence.observedEffect: Blue catfish consumed significantly more gizzard shad than blue crab.
evidence.novaApplicability: useful prey-context and Fish Guide evidence
evidence.limitations: Prey availability, handling and energetic density differ; not an environmental multiplier.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Fish grouped in 100-mm length bins from roughly 300 to 800 mm TL.
evidence.observedEffect: The 500-600 mm groups had the highest laboratory maximum-consumption estimates.
evidence.limitations: Only one representative fish was used in each length class above 500 mm; authors caution that individual behavior may explain the pattern.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 1,226 stomachs sampled in August at 22.3-29.6 C from four Virginia tidal rivers.
evidence.observedEffect: Estimated daily ration varied by river from 2.27% to 5.22% body weight per 24 h.
evidence.populationLocation: James, Pamunkey, Mattaponi, and Rappahannock rivers, Virginia
evidence.limitations: Estimates depend on evacuation/chronology modeling, prey identification, summer temperature and sampled times.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: August diet chronologies across four Virginia tidal rivers.
evidence.observedEffect: Peak stomach fullness occurred between 0900 and 1500 overall, but peak feeding time differed among rivers and the authors found no consistent universal diel pattern.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Stomach fullness and modeled feeding chronology
evidence.novaApplicability: high for rejecting a universal hourly bonus
evidence.limitations: August-only sampling; stomach evacuation and tidal movement can shift apparent peaks.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Field feeding chronologies in four tidal rivers.
evidence.observedEffect: Peak feeding appeared near the end of outgoing tide in the James, Pamunkey, and Rappahannock, but near the end of incoming tide in the Mattaponi; authors called for more research.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Modeled feeding chronology relative to tide
evidence.limitations: Four-river inconsistency and one August sampling window prevent a portable tide rule.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 16,110 stomachs across four Virginia tidal rivers.
evidence.observedEffect: Diet shifted from omnivory toward piscivory, with transition size varying by river roughly within 500-900 mm TL.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Diet composition, trophic level and prey occurrence
evidence.limitations: Diet composition is not feeding intensity or angling vulnerability; thresholds vary by river.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Tidal fresh, oligohaline and mesohaline reaches sampled across seasons.
evidence.observedEffect: Prey composition varied by season, salinity zone, fish size and river.
evidence.limitations: Does not isolate salinity as a causal feeding-rate effect; prey fields co-vary.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Accepted as Lepomis macrochirus; supplied and accepted names match.
evidence.observedEffect: No species-level name change affecting Northern Virginia was identified.
evidence.novaApplicability: Direct naming applicability; not a score input
evidence.limitations: Taxonomic identity does not imply behavioral uniformity among ecotypes.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 23 Bluegill captured at least once and 25 not captured, assessed by intermittent-flow respirometry.
evidence.observedEffect: Captured and uncaptured fish did not differ in standard or maximum metabolic rate, postexercise oxygen consumption, or recovery time.
evidence.novaApplicability: Direct null evidence against a metabolism-based vulnerability rule
evidence.limitations: Results are context-specific; they do not prove physiology never matters under other conditions.

evidence.variable: Winter dissolved oxygen, temperature, and current
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Backwater conditions with dissolved oxygen above/below 2 mg/L, temperature near/below 1°C, and current around/above 1 cm/s.
evidence.observedEffect: When oxygen exceeded 2 mg/L, Bluegill selected water above 1°C and little detectable current; under lower oxygen they moved toward higher oxygen even if colder or flowing.
evidence.limitations: Endpoint was movement/habitat, not feeding or hook-and-line catchability.

evidence.variable: Winter temperature, food, size, consumption, and survival
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Age-0 Bluegill, 4°C versus 9°C, food present/absent, small 20–30 mm versus large 50–60 mm total length.
evidence.observedEffect: Food-treated fish consumed roughly 2–4% body weight/day in warm treatments, about 1–2.5% for small fish in cold treatment, and about 0.4–0.8% for large fish in cold treatment; survival depended strongly on body size and condition.
evidence.novaApplicability: Shows temperature–size–food interaction, but not adult bite optimum
evidence.limitations: Juvenile winter survival and provided food cannot be translated into adult angling scores.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Repeated stomach-content sampling by hour of day in lake fishes including Bluegill.
evidence.observedEffect: Feeding periodicity and food uptake varied by hour in the studied lake population.
evidence.novaApplicability: Direct feeding endpoint but insufficiently portable for a universal clock rule
evidence.limitations: Full text was inaccessible and exact bluegill hourly peaks were not used as scoring thresholds.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Radioisotope-based estimate of daily Bluegill feeding rate.
evidence.observedEffect: The study demonstrated that daily consumption can be quantified, but did not provide a portable real-time environmental predictor for BiteMap.
evidence.limitations: No production rule is justified without detailed conditions and a portable predictor.

evidence.variable: Body size, prey profitability, and habitat use
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Field and experimental comparisons across Bluegill body sizes.
evidence.observedEffect: Foraging efficiency, prey choice, and profitable habitat differed with body size.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Foraging efficiency, diet, and habitat use
evidence.novaApplicability: Supports size/life-stage context, not a single universal bite-size curve
evidence.limitations: Abstract-only access and differing prey/habitats prevent numerical calibration here.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Early-summer colony nesting and male defense of eggs/fry.
evidence.observedEffect: Nest defense can produce strikes or increased local vulnerability without representing feeding motivation.
evidence.limitations: No direct experiment isolated feeding versus defense in hook-and-line catches.

evidence.variable: Atmospheric weather, moon, and natural-light folklore
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Barometric pressure, fronts, wind, ordinary rain, cloud cover, and moon phase.
evidence.observedEffect: No qualifying Bluegill study established direct natural-weather or lunar catchability effects after underwater light, temperature, oxygen, and habitat were separated.
evidence.limitations: The artificial-light experiment does not justify natural moon or cloud rules.

evidence.variable: Recent angling pressure, learning, and depletion
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Repeated recent angling exposure independent of removals and density.
evidence.observedEffect: Behavioral vulnerability studies show individual selectivity, but no qualifying study provided a portable short-term pressure-decay function separated from harvest depletion.
evidence.limitations: Capture history, population structure, refuge, and removal can all change observed catch rates.

evidence.variable: Regional occurrence, habitat, diet, and recreational use
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Virginia ponds, reservoirs, lakes, and slow-flowing waters, commonly near vegetation and cover.
evidence.observedEffect: Bluegill are broadly and intentionally targeted in Virginia; agency life history supports targetability and location context.
evidence.novaApplicability: High regional relevance; not an environmental catchability function
evidence.limitations: The account does not quantify short-term feeding probability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Juvenile Bluegill exposed at night to an intermittent 12 lx treatment in outdoor mesocosms over six weeks.
evidence.observedEffect: Intermittent high-intensity artificial light reduced prey-capture rate and strike rate relative to dark/steady treatments.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Capture rate, strike rate, and foraging behavior
evidence.novaApplicability: Direct feeding/attack evidence, but only for a narrow artificial-light condition
evidence.limitations: Do not generalize to moon phase, cloud cover, ordinary shoreline lighting, adults, or natural waters.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Steady nighttime treatments of 1, 4, or 12 lx compared with dark controls.
evidence.observedEffect: Steady light treatments showed no apparent effect on capture efficiency, capture rate, strike rate, or latency in the studied juvenile mesocosms.
evidence.novaApplicability: Direct null evidence within tested conditions
evidence.limitations: A null in this design does not prove no effects at other spectra, intensities, cover, prey, or life stages.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Larval Bluegill tested across sediment turbidity and light levels; low-light portions fell below roughly 450 lx.
evidence.observedEffect: Sediment turbidity reduced consumption primarily under lower light; at high light, prey biomass consumed did not differ with turbidity although prey size selection changed.
evidence.novaApplicability: Mechanistic context; not an adult bite rule
evidence.limitations: Larvae, experimental prey, and illumination differ from adult recreational fisheries; do not create a universal NTU curve.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Wild juvenile Bluegill captured by angling versus beach seining, then behaviorally tested.
evidence.observedEffect: Angled fish were more timid and carried fewer ectoparasites than seined fish.
evidence.populationLocation: Ontario field capture plus laboratory tests
evidence.novaApplicability: Direct catchability association but not a real-time environmental input
evidence.limitations: Capture method can create sampling bias; behavior was measured after capture and may be population-specific.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Large outdoor-pool angling trial with individually tagged, previously behavior-tested Bluegill.
evidence.observedEffect: The timidity relationship from the capture-method comparison did not carry over consistently; bolder individuals were more likely to be angled in open water away from refuge in the pool experiment.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Angling outcome versus prior boldness score
evidence.novaApplicability: Contradictory context demonstrating no universal personality rule
evidence.limitations: Experimental setting and refuge geometry may drive the direction of the effect.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Naturalistic experimental pond; captured and uncaptured Bluegill assessed for sociability.
evidence.observedEffect: More sociable Bluegill were selectively captured by recreational angling.
evidence.novaApplicability: Direct vulnerability evidence but the trait is not operationally observable in BiteMap
evidence.limitations: Population, social environment, lure, and angling protocol limit transfer.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Same naturalistic pond experiment.
evidence.observedEffect: Aggression or dominance did not provide the same clear capture association as sociability.
evidence.limitations: Abstract-only access limits detailed effect-size verification.

evidence.variable: regional targetability, native status and ecology
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Virginia brook-trout resources, including native southern Appalachian populations.
evidence.observedEffect: Confirms high intentional targetability and the importance of wild-versus-stocked and genetic context.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Distribution, management status, genetics and life history
evidence.limitations: Habitat and thermal preference are not feeding or catchability optima.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Three wild brook-trout strains exposed to different exploitation levels in Michigan.
evidence.observedEffect: The faster-growing East Branch Fox strain was caught more readily than the compared Au Sable strains.
evidence.limitations: Founder effects, growth, behavior and prior selection were not cleanly separated; not portable to Virginia genetics without validation.

evidence.variable: hook type, active/passive presentation and catchability
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 201 stream-dwelling brook trout captured with circle and J hooks under active/passive methods.
evidence.observedEffect: Hooking method and hook type affected capture and injury outcomes.
evidence.limitations: Gear/presentation belongs in Fish Guide; it does not establish an environmental bite score.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Brook trout acclimated across warm temperatures in a controlled experiment.
evidence.observedEffect: Upper growth performance and stress responses changed with temperature.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Growth, endocrine and physiological stress endpoints
evidence.limitations: Growth and stress are not feeding or catchability; do not treat the growth limit as a bite optimum.

evidence.variable: season, diel period, light and activity
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 17-month telemetry in an ice-covered Newfoundland lake.
evidence.observedEffect: Depth, movement and range varied with season, temperature, light and time of day.
evidence.limitations: Lake/ice environment and movement endpoint prevent a bite-time rule.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Fingerling brook trout given laboratory dissolved-oxygen gradients.
evidence.observedEffect: Fish distribution shifted across oxygen gradients, demonstrating avoidance/selection behavior.
evidence.limitations: Occupancy is not feed intake or catchability; acclimation and temperature interactions limit transfer.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Brook trout exposed to oxygen treatments in a laboratory experiment.
evidence.observedEffect: Activity responded to oxygen concentration.
evidence.limitations: Activity is not feeding, and direction cannot be converted to catchability without direct linkage.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Virginia put-and-take waters with trout species pooled.
evidence.observedEffect: Observed catch was fastest on stocking day, while catch and effort depended on site, month and time since stocking.
evidence.limitations: May reflect accessibility and angler concentration rather than feeding.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Post-stocking intervals through 30 days in pooled Virginia trout data.
evidence.observedEffect: Catch rates after the initial pulse remained near 1 trout per angler-hour instead of declining monotonically.
evidence.limitations: Species pooled; overlapping stocking and harvest may mask local patterns.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Stocked brook, rainbow and brown trout in an Adirondack river; summer exceeded 20 C with cold refuges.
evidence.observedEffect: Estimated angler catch was highest for brook trout (72%); warm conditions did not lower catch because refuges concentrated fish.
evidence.limitations: Catch concentration is not feeding; species differed in survival and movement.

evidence.variable: temperature by competitor interaction on feeding
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Brook trout alone, paired with brook trout, or paired with creek chub at 18, 20 and 22 C in flow-through tanks.
evidence.observedEffect: As temperature increased, brook-trout feeding and aggression declined significantly when paired with creek chub.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Pellets consumed, feeding latency, aggression and space use
evidence.novaApplicability: mechanistically relevant to warm lower-elevation streams with creek chub
evidence.limitations: Artificial pellets and dyads; temperature effect depended on competitor identity and cannot be a universal brook-trout curve.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Same 18, 20 and 22 C treatments across solitary and paired combinations.
evidence.observedEffect: Space use and dominance shifted by pairing treatment; solitary and conspecific responses differed from brook-trout/creek-chub pairs.
evidence.limitations: Requires local competitor presence/abundance; movement and aggression should not be double-counted as feeding.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Artificial stream at 12.0 +/- 0.5 C, about 49 lx, 0.06 m/s; turbidity from <3 to >40 NTU; hatchery fish mean length about 126 mm.
evidence.observedEffect: Turbidity had no significant effect on mean daily prey consumption.
evidence.populationLocation: Artificial stream, West Virginia research context
evidence.novaApplicability: good Appalachian mechanistic relevance, limited life stage
evidence.limitations: Does not cover adult angling, higher turbidity, natural prey drift, or different light/current.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Same <3 to >40 NTU artificial-stream experiment.
evidence.observedEffect: Growth declined as turbidity increased while activity and foraging strategy shifted from drift feeding toward active searching.
evidence.limitations: Growth cost occurred without reduced consumption; converting growth to bite would reverse the actual feeding endpoint.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Radio-tagged brook trout in a complex West Virginia riverscape.
evidence.observedEffect: Movement and location were associated with maximum temperature and distance to cold-water sources; fish used thermal refugia and no tracked fish were observed above the reported high-temperature envelope.
evidence.limitations: Movement and occupancy are not feeding or catchability; telemetry detection and system geometry matter.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Current catalog status
evidence.observedEffect: Accepted as Ameiurus nebulosus (Lesueur, 1819); original type locality was the Delaware River near Philadelphia.
evidence.limitations: Not a predictive study.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Day versus night under winter experimental conditions
evidence.observedEffect: Predation occurred almost exclusively at night; hunting periodicity was classified as nocturnal.
evidence.limitations: Winter-specific laboratory evidence; do not universalize to all seasons, clarity levels, or sizes.

evidence.variable: winter field feeding and heated effluent
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Heated power-plant discharge versus a reference pond near 2 C
evidence.observedEffect: Fish in the heated discharge fed, whereas fish from the approximately 2 C reference water did not in sampled stomachs.
evidence.limitations: Separate sites confound temperature with habitat and effluent; sample-specific absence is not universal cessation.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: No-flow versus flowing flume with a gelatin odor source
evidence.observedEffect: 100% located the odor source without flow versus 57% under flow; swimming paths differed.
evidence.limitations: Orientation is not ingestion or hook-and-line catchability; no natural-flow threshold.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Lake Opinicon, monthly May-November stomach sampling relative to food availability
evidence.observedEffect: Brown bullheads were broadly opportunistic; chironomids were consistently consumed and amphipods were emphasized when abundant.
evidence.limitations: Diet composition does not quantify a weather or temperature bite response.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 278 fish from seven Central-Eastern European lakes
evidence.observedEffect: Twenty food categories were found; detritus, Chironomidae, plants, and macrofauna were frequent; diet varied with lake trophic status.
evidence.limitations: European invasive populations; habitat and prey availability are intertwined.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Temperature experiment documented in primary literature
evidence.observedEffect: No growth optimum was converted into a bite optimum.
evidence.lifeStage: year-0 and older fish reported in metadata/secondary citations
evidence.limitations: Exact full text not inspected; growth is score-ineligible here.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Maryland freshwater hotspot accounts list brown bullhead in regional waters
evidence.observedEffect: The species is available to Mid-Atlantic anglers and is a plausible intentional target.
evidence.limitations: Not effort-standardized and not a catchability predictor.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: At least 28 days captivity; 18 C or 25 C treatment; 25 C fish ramped 1 C/day for 7 days then held 14 days; 3 ppt salinity; 3-h chironomid trials at prey densities 2-500
evidence.observedEffect: The design represents sustained acclimation rather than an acute temperature shock.
evidence.limitations: Artificial salinity and captivity; one prey type; Canadian population; not hook-and-line catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 18 C versus 25 C after sustained acclimation
evidence.observedEffect: Attack rate was 1.27 +/- 0.05 at 18 C and 0.59 +/- 0.05 at 25 C; the model comparison was significant (p < 0.001).
evidence.limitations: Do not infer a smooth curve or universal optimum from two treatments.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 18 C versus 25 C after sustained acclimation
evidence.observedEffect: Handling time was 0.005 +/- 0.000 h at 18 C and 0.013 +/- 0.001 h at 25 C; the model comparison was significant (p < 0.001).
evidence.limitations: Units and fitted-model context must be preserved; not a lure-handling result.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 18 C versus 25 C
evidence.observedEffect: Estimated maximum feeding rate declined from 209 prey/h to 75 prey/h; FRR declined from 265 (244-288) to 44 (37-53).
evidence.limitations: Calibration candidate only; single prey type, two temperatures, laboratory conditions.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 18 C versus 25 C across prey-density treatments
evidence.observedEffect: Consumption at 25 C was significantly lower across nearly the entire prey-density range tested.
evidence.limitations: Does not prove that all natural populations feed best at 18 C.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Seven-week feeding-trial span; 18 C and 25 C
evidence.observedEffect: Brown bullhead condition increased at 18 C but did not change significantly at 25 C; HSI did not differ by temperature.
evidence.limitations: Condition is not feeding rate or catchability; use only as context and adversarial check.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Controlled winter test at 3 C
evidence.observedEffect: Predation occurred at temperatures as low as 3 C.
evidence.lifeStage: young; conference abstract reported mean 123 +/- 4 mm TL
evidence.limitations: Small European non-native fish and winter lab conditions; no basis for a universal field threshold.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 3 C versus 4.5 C
evidence.observedEffect: Modeled potential predation impact showed a strong increase in resource consumption from 3 C to 4.5 C.
evidence.limitations: Narrow 1.5 C contrast and non-native juvenile population; direction may not transfer quantitatively.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Virginia wild brown-trout populations and major tailwater fisheries.
evidence.observedEffect: Confirms intentional regional targeting and broad waterbody contexts.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Distribution, management status and life history
evidence.limitations: Not a feeding or catchability curve.

evidence.variable: absolute temperature, body size and feeding capacity
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Brown trout 9-302 g tested from approximately 3.8 to 18.1 C.
evidence.observedEffect: Maximum daily ration and feeding rate depended on temperature and body mass.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Meal number, maximum food consumed and feeding rate
evidence.novaApplicability: useful calibration context but not a simple field optimum
evidence.limitations: Equations, acclimation and ration design must be reviewed before implementation; no short-term trend or catchability endpoint.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Laboratory combinations of body weight, water temperature and ration.
evidence.observedEffect: Energetic allocation changed jointly with temperature, body size and ration.
evidence.limitations: Growth and metabolism are not hook-and-line catchability; exact equations were not fully verified in this run.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 22 radio-tagged trout, 268-446 mm, across 47 24-hour tracking periods in a southern Appalachian river.
evidence.observedEffect: Most movement was short and pool-centered; timing varied by season, with sunrise, sunset and night movements depending on season.
evidence.novaApplicability: high geographic relevance, wrong endpoint for bite
evidence.limitations: Movement is not feeding; detection and sample size limit hourly inference.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Telemetry in a southern Appalachian river.
evidence.observedEffect: Seasonal movements and habitat shifts occurred, including spawning-related movement.
evidence.limitations: Cannot become a monthly bite curve or flow effect without feeding/catch data.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: November-March in a groundwater-dominated Minnesota stream; fish size classes sampled.
evidence.observedEffect: Brown trout continued feeding and smaller fish showed measurable winter growth.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Diet, ration proxies, growth and condition
evidence.limitations: Groundwater temperature stability and prey community differ from NOVA; feeding does not equal angler catch.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Free-ranging wild and hatchery brown trout observed in a Pennsylvania stream.
evidence.observedEffect: Foraging tactics and efficiency differed with origin and experience.
evidence.limitations: Older study and site-specific prey drift; does not yield a single environment multiplier.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Virginia put-and-take waters, pooled trout species.
evidence.observedEffect: Catch was fastest on stocking day, with site, month and time since stocking affecting observed catch and effort.
evidence.novaApplicability: high regional relevance but species pooled
evidence.limitations: Access and effort can explain part of the pattern.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Post-stocking intervals through 30 days, pooled trout species.
evidence.observedEffect: Catch rates remained near 1 trout per angler-hour after the initial pulse rather than showing a simple monotonic collapse.
evidence.novaApplicability: high for rejecting a generic decay rule
evidence.limitations: Pooled species and overlapping stockings.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Stocked brook, rainbow and brown trout in a thermally marginal Adirondack river.
evidence.observedEffect: Estimated angler catch differed strongly among species; brown trout had the lowest estimated fraction caught, and heat did not uniformly reduce catch where refuges concentrated fish.
evidence.limitations: Recovery fraction is not intrinsic catchability without equal abundance, survival and behavior.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Four 3-day trips in a lightly fished and a more regularly fished New Zealand backcountry river.
evidence.observedEffect: After fish were caught/released or merely disturbed, trout were less likely to remain visible or readily approachable on following days; naive fish were more catchable.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Sightings, behavioral responses and hook-and-line captures
evidence.populationLocation: Owen and Ugly rivers, New Zealand
evidence.limitations: Remote clear-water sight-fishing, low fish density and skilled anglers limit transfer; disturbance and actual hooking were partly combined.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Previously fished trout in the New Zealand rivers.
evidence.observedEffect: More pressured trout were more likely to require smaller or lower-profile flies and were more easily scared.
evidence.limitations: Presentation finding is gear-specific and should not become an environmental score.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Hatchery-reared brown trout measured for exploratory behavior before angling.
evidence.observedEffect: More explorative individuals were more vulnerable to capture.
evidence.novaApplicability: population context, not an API weather input
evidence.limitations: Hatchery origin and individual personality are rarely observed; selection can change populations.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 0, 150, 300, 450 and 600 mg/L suspended sediment after macrophyte-control disturbance.
evidence.observedEffect: Feeding was reduced by about 22% at 450 mg/L and 31% at 600 mg/L relative to control.
evidence.limitations: Units are mg/L suspended sediment, not NTU; extreme pulse and experimental prey conditions limit transfer.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Up to 600 mg/L suspended sediment in the same experiment.
evidence.observedEffect: Oxygen consumption did not show the same decline as feeding.
evidence.limitations: Physiological null result does not negate feeding reduction.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Original description as Silurus punctatus Rafinesque, 1818; currently valid as Ictalurus punctatus
evidence.observedEffect: The accepted scientific name remains Ictalurus punctatus. No taxonomic split requiring a different Northern Virginia name was identified.
evidence.populationLocation: Type locality Ohio River; taxonomic record is range-wide
evidence.novaApplicability: Directly applicable to naming; not a biological score input

sourceLocator.section: Species record for punctatus, Silurus Rafinesque

evidence.limitations: Taxonomic validity does not establish that all hatchery strains, crosses, or hybrids have identical behavior.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 15.7-31.7 C and 30, 70, or 100% air saturation
evidence.observedEffect: Feed intake increased with temperature across the tested range and declined progressively as oxygen fell from 100 to 30% saturation; feed intake was significantly lowest at 15.7 C and highest at 30 C with 100% saturation in the tested treatments.
evidence.populationLocation: Controlled aquaria simulating southeastern United States spring and fall
evidence.lifeStage: Juveniles initially about 15 g and 10-12 cm
evidence.novaApplicability: Mechanistically useful; juvenile aquaculture experiment, no descending thermal limb
evidence.limitations: The study could not produce the supra-optimal descending limb. Growth values and the 30 C treatment must not be converted into a wild adult bite optimum.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 100, 60, and 36% oxygen saturation
evidence.observedEffect: Food consumption and growth were substantially reduced at 36% saturation while survival remained 100%, separating feeding impairment from lethality.
evidence.novaApplicability: Supports low-oxygen feeding penalty; percent saturation should be preserved
evidence.limitations: Only the abstract was accessed. Percent saturation varies in mg/L with temperature, pressure, and salinity, so no universal mg/L conversion is supplied.

evidence.variable: Minimum daily dissolved oxygen and feed consumption
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Warm earthen ponds; feed began decreasing below approximately 3.0 mg/L and declined rapidly below 2.5 mg/L; at 1.7 mg/L feed was 44.1% below the high-oxygen control
evidence.observedEffect: Lower nightly minimum dissolved oxygen reduced the amount of feed consumed, with a nonlinear increase in feeding loss at severe minima.
evidence.novaApplicability: Useful for warm ponds and reservoirs with nightly oxygen minima; not a universal river threshold

sourceLocator.section: Discussion - feed consumption response to minimum dissolved oxygen

evidence.limitations: Aeration treatments, stocked density, pellet feeding, and warm pond conditions differ from wild Northern Virginia systems. Use only within compatible warmwater contexts.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Low-flow channel conditions versus elevated flow connecting river channel, oxbow, and floodplain habitats
evidence.observedEffect: During low flow, tracked fish largely remained in-channel and moved less than 1 km. During elevated flow, fish moved into or remained within floodplain-connected reaches; several entered floodplain or oxbow habitat, and one moved approximately 40 km.
evidence.novaApplicability: Qualitatively relevant to connected river-floodplain systems; less direct for confined Northern Virginia reaches
evidence.limitations: Movement and habitat access do not establish increased feeding or hook-and-line catchability. Absolute flows are system-specific.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: September 2014-April 2016, 24-hour locations of 27 Channel Catfish in a 16-km lower Wabash River reach
evidence.observedEffect: Movement was greatest at night across seasons; displacement was greatest in fall and lower in spring. Activity increased as water temperature decreased, while gauge height was not a significant predictor. Bank and riprap use varied by season and day-night period.
evidence.novaApplicability: Large Midwestern river context; useful for habitat and diel context but conflicts with feeding-temperature studies
evidence.limitations: Only the repository abstract was accessible. Increased movement during cooling does not mean increased feeding; exact results require full-text audit.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Juveniles 20-56 mm observed across diel periods in natural habitat
evidence.observedEffect: Juveniles were more abundant during evening and night and fed mainly during darkness.
evidence.novaApplicability: Low for adult angling forecasts; supports life-stage-specific flexibility
evidence.limitations: Only the abstract was accessed. Juvenile behavior and study geography cannot override adult Conowingo feeding chronology.

evidence.variable: Salinity tolerance of early life stages
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Egg and larval exposures up to approximately 16 ppt; hatching success declined around 8 ppt and post-yolk-sac survival was limited near 9-10 ppt
evidence.observedEffect: Early life stages tolerated some brackish exposure, but development and survival declined as salinity increased.
evidence.novaApplicability: Relevant only to reproduction in tidal-brackish waters, not adult catchability
evidence.limitations: The full report was accessed, but this record concerns early life stages. Adult salinity preference, feeding, and angling catchability were not measured.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Multiple Channel Catfish strains, crossbreeds, and Channel Catfish x Blue Catfish hybrids in controlled ponds
evidence.observedEffect: Angling vulnerability differed among genetic groups; hybrids and some crosses were more catchable than parental or comparison strains.
evidence.populationLocation: Controlled pond experiments in the southeastern United States
evidence.novaApplicability: Important applicability warning for stocked Northern Virginia fisheries
evidence.limitations: Only the abstract was accessed. Genetic composition in individual Northern Virginia stockings is often unknown, so no environmental multiplier is justified.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Equal numbers of marked Channel Catfish and hybrids stocked into four urban ponds on three occasions; five daily creel surveys over two weeks
evidence.observedEffect: Nearly five times more Channel Catfish than hybrids were harvested in the first daily survey after stocking. Channel Catfish harvest declined significantly by the second survey, and later surveys showed no significant type difference.
evidence.populationLocation: Four urban put-and-take fisheries in Texas
evidence.lifeStage: Harvestable fish around 305 mm total length
evidence.novaApplicability: Strong for managed put-and-take ponds immediately after stocking; weak for wild rivers and established populations
evidence.limitations: Only the abstract was accessed. The decline may combine harvest depletion, dispersal, acclimation, angler effort, and behavioral change; it is not evidence of a feeding surge.

evidence.variable: Seasonal angler catch in Mid-Atlantic waters
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Pennsylvania creel surveys from 1986-2002; reservoir catches greatest July-October and river catches greatest June-September
evidence.observedEffect: Observed angler catches were seasonally concentrated in warmer months, with different timing between reservoirs and rivers.
evidence.novaApplicability: Good regional context; not a per-fish environmental function
evidence.limitations: Catch totals confound fish abundance, effort, access, gear, harvest, and daytime survey design. Use as categorical seasonal context only.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Virginia rivers, reservoirs, ponds, and warmwater habitats; spawning generally April-June
evidence.observedEffect: Channel Catfish are opportunistic feeders using fish, invertebrates, and other foods. Adults use varied still and flowing waters. Spawning occurs in concealed cavities, with males preparing and guarding nests.
evidence.limitations: The account does not quantify short-term feeding or hook-and-line catchability functions.

evidence.variable: Feeding mode, diel flexibility, and spawning synthesis
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Species-life-history synthesis for southeastern Channel Catfish
evidence.observedEffect: Channel Catfish use taste and olfaction, feed near the bottom, and may feed by day or night. Spawning is associated with warm water and cavities, with male parental care.
evidence.novaApplicability: Mechanistically relevant for guide and habitat context
evidence.limitations: The document includes aquaculture growth guidance. Growth optima and farm-management thresholds are not bite optima.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 2016 Virginia angler survey and statewide stocked fisheries
evidence.observedEffect: Fifty-four percent of surveyed Virginia anglers reported specifically fishing for catfish; reported catfish effort occurred in small impoundments (23%), large impoundments (27%), warmwater streams (38%), and private lakes (12%). The plan notes stocked Channel Catfish are vulnerable to anglers.
evidence.lifeStage: Catchable stocked fish and mixed wild fish
evidence.limitations: Survey percentages describe angler participation and habitat choice, not per-fish environmental catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Three-hour stomach collections across 24 hours in July-November
evidence.observedEffect: Freshly ingested food occurred at every collection. Feeding began increasing around 0400, reached a maximum between 1500 and 1800, and was heavier during daylight in the studied reservoir.
evidence.lifeStage: Subadult and adult fish represented in 798 stomachs
evidence.novaApplicability: High regional relevance, but one reservoir and one seasonal study
evidence.limitations: Stomach chronology is not angling catchability. Gear, prey availability, reservoir operations, and season may alter diel timing.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: July-November; water temperature declined from approximately 82 F in July to 53 F in November
evidence.observedEffect: The percentage of empty stomachs increased as the season cooled, consistent with declining feeding intensity, while feeding did not cease.

sourceLocator.section: Food and feeding chronology; seasonal stomach fullness

evidence.limitations: Temperature covaried with month, prey, and reservoir conditions. Empty-stomach frequency is not a calibrated catchability curve.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Average feed consumption was approximately 0.7% body weight at 15.7-21.1 C, 0.3% at 10.1-15.6 C, and 0.1% at 10 C or lower; voluntary feeding was observed down to 7 C
evidence.observedEffect: Feed intake was progressively reduced at colder temperatures, but Channel Catfish continued accepting feed at 7 C.
evidence.populationLocation: Mississippi earthen ponds and indoor winter-feeding vats
evidence.novaApplicability: Mechanistically relevant; commercial feed and southern aquaculture conditions limit direct transfer
evidence.limitations: Rations were management treatments, not unrestricted wild foraging. Percent-body-weight values must not be interpreted as BiteMap score multipliers.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Winter days classified by increasing, decreasing, or unchanged water temperature within approximately 7-21.1 C
evidence.observedEffect: Feed consumption was significantly greater on warming or thermally stable days than on cooling days.
evidence.populationLocation: Mississippi winter aquaculture ponds and vats
evidence.novaApplicability: Plausible short-term mechanism for Mid-Atlantic winter waters; magnitude not portable
evidence.limitations: The result involved offered commercial feed and managed ponds. It does not establish a universal front or barometric-pressure rule.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Cyclic temperature treatments of 23-27, 27-31, and 31-35 C
evidence.observedEffect: Feed consumption was greatest at 27-31 C and declined in the 31-35 C treatment.
evidence.novaApplicability: Direction of extreme-heat effect is useful; juvenile aquaculture values are not a wild adult bite optimum
evidence.limitations: Do not set 27-31 C as an optimum bite range. Fish size, ration, cycling regime, and captive density differ from Northern Virginia fisheries.

evidence.variable: Movement versus feeding under high heat
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Cyclic 31-35 C treatment compared with cooler treatments
evidence.observedEffect: General activity was greatest in the hottest treatment even though feed consumption declined and survival was lower, demonstrating that movement can increase while feeding performance worsens.
evidence.novaApplicability: Strong adversarial warning; exact treatment not directly transferable

sourceLocator.section: Results - Feed Consumption, Activity, and Survival; Discussion

evidence.limitations: Activity was observed in tanks and may include stress behavior. It must not be interpreted as higher catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Widespread Virginia populations and long-standing recreational fishery.
evidence.observedEffect: Confirms deliberate hook-and-line targeting and broad habitat availability.
evidence.limitations: Agency natural history does not define bite multipliers.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Repeated experimental hook-and-line selection.
evidence.observedEffect: Boldness/resource-acquisition behavior was associated with greater vulnerability and could be selected against.
evidence.limitations: Not an environmental input available to BiteMap.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Repeated corn-pellet conditioning in semi-natural enclosures.
evidence.observedEffect: Carp formed feeding aggregations and accepted familiar bait, supporting prebaiting as a presentation tactic.
evidence.limitations: Management-control context, not an environmental bite coefficient.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Multi-water recreational catch/stock records.
evidence.observedEffect: Catch reflected stocking, abundance and fishery practice; stock-catch relationships do not isolate per-fish appetite.
evidence.limitations: Effort, regulations, stocking and harvest confound seasonality.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: North American occurrence and introduced status.
evidence.observedEffect: Confirms broad ecological plasticity and variable population histories.
evidence.limitations: Plasticity argues against exact cross-region threshold transfer.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Searches for barometric pressure, fronts, lunar phase, ordinary rain, wind and cloud effects.
evidence.observedEffect: No qualifying direct common-carp feeding or standardized angling effect was verified independent of temperature, light or effort.
evidence.limitations: Absence of evidence does not prove no effect.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Searches for species-specific intake/catchability at measured mg/L.
evidence.observedEffect: Tolerance and aquaculture physiology studies were available, but no portable wild feeding or hook-and-line coefficient qualified.
evidence.limitations: Do not convert survival/tolerance into bite score.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Adults 630-850 g and juveniles 61-91 g tested across 4-34 C; explicit intake values reported at 6, 14, 28 and 34 C.
evidence.observedEffect: Daily ration was very low at 6 C, increased strongly by 14 C, peaked at 28 C, and declined at 34 C; juveniles consumed a larger body-mass percentage than adults.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Daily feed intake as percent body mass
evidence.novaApplicability: direct endpoint but strain, diet and culture transfer limits
evidence.limitations: Do not fit a smooth universal curve from four highlighted temperatures or transfer exact percentages to wild North American carp.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Across tested temperatures, 24-hour feed observations.
evidence.observedEffect: Two principal feeding peaks occurred around 08:00-11:00 and 19:00-23:00; below 10 C the evening peak extended toward 04:00.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Hourly distribution of daily feed intake
evidence.limitations: Feeding schedule, photoperiod and husbandry can entrain timing; not a universal clock.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Juveniles 90-105 mm tested at 16, 20, 24 and 28 C with two foods.
evidence.observedEffect: Foraging/feeding increased from 16 to 24 C and did not increase further from 24 to 28 C; growth was depressed at 16 and 28 C relative to intermediate treatments.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Feeding rates, functional response and growth
evidence.limitations: Growth and feeding endpoints must remain separate; 24 C should not become a universal adult optimum.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Direct hooking and release followed by sham-rig/bait trials within hours and again over several days.
evidence.observedEffect: Directly hooked carp became more cautious and less vulnerable; avoidance persisted at least 5-7 days in the study.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Rig approach, bait ingestion and recapture vulnerability
evidence.novaApplicability: high mechanistic relevance; field magnitude uncertain
evidence.limitations: Group history, bait type and captive setting limit numerical transfer.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Naive observers witnessed conspecific capture-and-release.
evidence.observedEffect: Socially exposed fish showed short-term caution toward baited sham rigs, but persistence was weaker and less consistent than direct experience.
evidence.limitations: Population-level effect depends on visibility, group structure and repeated exposure.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Previously directly or socially exposed carp retested 7 and 14 months after initial trial.
evidence.observedEffect: No convincing hook avoidance remained beyond about seven months; directly exposed fish briefly took longer to approach at seven months but ingestion did not differ over the 600-s trial.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Approach latency and bait ingestion near sham rig
evidence.limitations: Does not establish the shorter decay shape between one week and seven months.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Wild individually tracked common carp exposed to baited locations.
evidence.observedEffect: Encountering bait was necessary but did not by itself explain individual vulnerability; spatial encounter metrics were not sufficient predictors of capture.
evidence.limitations: Other traits, feeding motivation and bait acceptance still matter.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Domesticated mirror carp versus less-domesticated scaled/wild-type carp in experimental environments.
evidence.observedEffect: Domesticated carp were more vulnerable to angling and showed greater food intake/bolder foraging.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Capture vulnerability, food intake and behavior
evidence.limitations: Virginia populations have unknown ancestry and mixed domestication history.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Fairfax County stream surveys and agency description.
evidence.observedEffect: Creek chub are locally common and grow large enough to be caught on artificial lures; Maryland notes they readily strike trout lures.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Regional occurrence and intentional hook-and-line practicality
evidence.limitations: Not a standardized CPUE study.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Two-week summer mark-recapture in a low-gradient sand stream.
evidence.observedEffect: About 44% changed habitat patches; median movement was approximately 49 m and cover influenced patch use.
evidence.limitations: Movement and cover occupancy do not establish feeding.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Co-occurring brook trout and creek chub in oligotrophic Quebec lakes.
evidence.observedEffect: Species partitioned resources and habitat; interactions varied with community context.
evidence.limitations: Lake results should not set stream bite rules.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Direct feeding experiments included temperature but only within competitor designs.
evidence.observedEffect: No portable single-species thermal feeding optimum was verified.
evidence.limitations: Competition, appetite and trout stress are intertwined.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Searches for measured oxygen/turbidity feeding or hook-and-line effects.
evidence.observedEffect: No qualifying direct creek-chub coefficient was verified.
evidence.limitations: Do not infer from occurrence in tolerant streams.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Pressure, fronts, moon phase, wind, cloud and rainfall searches.
evidence.observedEffect: No qualifying direct creek-chub feeding or catchability study was verified.
evidence.limitations: Absence of evidence is not proof of no biological effect.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Spawning, summer diet and movement evidence.
evidence.observedEffect: No direct numerical month-by-month per-fish activity curve qualified.
evidence.limitations: Do not transform seasonal observations into monthly scores.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Summer field sampling in a Minnesota stream.
evidence.observedEffect: Feeding was most intense in early evening and least intense in the morning.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Stomach fullness/feeding intensity by diel interval
evidence.novaApplicability: moderate transfer to similar small streams
evidence.limitations: Single region and summer; terrestrial prey drift and light may be mechanisms.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Summer sampling across the study period.
evidence.observedEffect: Feeding intensity declined as summer progressed.
evidence.limitations: Calendar timing, prey availability, temperature and fish condition were not separated.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Summer diet observations.
evidence.observedEffect: Food composition broadly reflected prey availability, with creek chub using aquatic and terrestrial prey.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Diet composition and environmental prey samples
evidence.limitations: Diet occurrence does not establish bite response to weather.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Mink River spawning in mid-to-late May; water shallower than 25 cm and current faster than 15 cm/s.
evidence.observedEffect: Spawning occurred in shallow, relatively fast water and habitats differed by age.
evidence.limitations: Current used for spawning is not a feeding or catchability optimum.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Fish tested at 18, 20 and 22 C alone and with brook trout.
evidence.observedEffect: Warming changed competitive feeding and aggression; creek chub retained or gained relative advantage while brook-trout feeding declined in paired trials.
evidence.novaApplicability: mechanistically relevant but competitor abundance is required
evidence.limitations: Does not support a simple creek-chub temperature bonus when alone.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 3-26 C experiments with creek chub, brook trout and brown trout.
evidence.observedEffect: Creek chub competitive success increased at warm treatments, becoming dominant against trout around 22-26 C.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Food consumption and aggression in paired trials
evidence.limitations: Warm temperatures also stressed trout; relative dominance is not absolute feeding optimum.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Cortisol challenge in mesocosm and natural stream trials.
evidence.observedEffect: No clear difference in fine-scale movement, larger movement or diel activity was detected after the short-term cortisol treatment.
evidence.limitations: Feeding and angling were not measured; mortality effects occurred later.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Repeated boldness, exploration and activity assays across populations.
evidence.observedEffect: Behavioral traits were repeatable; larger individuals tended to be less active and population differences occurred.
evidence.limitations: Personality is not a real-time environmental input or direct catchability endpoint.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Virginia rivers and streams; adults may exceed 15-20 inches.
evidence.observedEffect: Virginia DWR describes deliberate ultralight and fly-fishing for an aggressive, hard-fighting native fish.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Intentional recreational targeting and regional distribution
evidence.limitations: Agency feature is not a standardized catchability experiment.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Agency accounts list small jigs, spinners, plugs, flies and live bait.
evidence.observedEffect: Fallfish willingly strike diverse presentations and are intentionally catchable on light tackle.
evidence.limitations: No controlled gear comparison or environmental coefficient.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Searches for short-term warming/cooling effects on feeding or hook-and-line catchability.
evidence.observedEffect: No qualifying species-specific direct study was verified.
evidence.limitations: Absence of evidence does not prove no response.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Searches for measured mg/L effects on feeding/catchability.
evidence.observedEffect: No qualifying direct fallfish feeding or angling coefficient was verified.
evidence.limitations: Do not infer from habitat presence or tolerance.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Barometric pressure, fronts, moon phase, wind, rainfall and cloud searches.
evidence.observedEffect: No qualifying direct species-specific feeding or standardized catchability effect was verified.
evidence.limitations: Angler lore is not evidence; absence does not establish no biological effect.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Regional natural history, spawning and prey studies.
evidence.observedEffect: No direct month-by-month per-fish feeding or catchability curve was verified.
evidence.limitations: Seasons and availability cannot substitute for direct activity measurement.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: One 24-hour summer sampling period in the Salmon River, New York.
evidence.observedEffect: Fallfish displayed a distinct feeding peak; supporting study materials place the peak late in the day/evening.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Stomach fullness/food consumption over diel intervals
evidence.novaApplicability: moderate ecological similarity but single river and season
evidence.limitations: Exact clock time, water clarity, prey drift and season may not transfer.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Same summer 24-hour study.
evidence.observedEffect: Terrestrial invertebrates comprised about 30% of fallfish food and diet overlap with other cyprinids was moderate.
evidence.limitations: Diet composition does not establish lure response or a universal activity multiplier.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Spawning observed when water reached approximately 14.4 C in Massachusetts.
evidence.observedEffect: Spawning began at the observed temperature; eggs hatched in 138-144 hours at 17.0 +/- 0.5 C.
evidence.limitations: Spawning threshold is not a feeding optimum or catchability rule.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Seasonal stomach sampling in Massachusetts.
evidence.observedEffect: Fallfish were omnivorous and consumed a broad range of aquatic and terrestrial food items.
evidence.limitations: Occurrence does not measure feeding rate.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 647 fallfish in autumn 2007-2008; size groups below 100 mm, 100-149 mm, and at least 150 mm.
evidence.observedEffect: Salmon-egg contribution increased above 100 mm; the largest group had 86.1% eggs in diet.
evidence.novaApplicability: low for NOVA because Pacific salmon egg pulse is absent
evidence.limitations: Highly unusual prey subsidy; do not create a generic large-fish feeding bonus.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: May versus June, 2009-2012; fallfish estimate available for 2009.
evidence.observedEffect: Predation on Chinook parr was higher in May than June; fallfish were estimated to consume 2.9 million parr in 2009.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Predation estimates from diet and prey abundance
evidence.novaApplicability: surrogate for prey pulses, not NOVA calendar scoring
evidence.limitations: Salmon emergence and hatchery context are absent in NOVA; abundance and prey availability confound per-fish intake.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Six sites in a warming Quebec boreal river.
evidence.observedEffect: Fallfish had a narrower habitat niche, were more abundant than brook trout, and both diets were dominated by aquatic insects.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Capture, habitat, stomach contents and stable isotopes
evidence.novaApplicability: context for warm-water expansion and prey overlap
evidence.limitations: Habitat occupancy and abundance are not bite probability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Virginia account contrasts southern river/stream populations with northern lake/pond populations.
evidence.observedEffect: Waterbody type and geography differ across the range.
evidence.limitations: Descriptive account, not quantified feeding evidence.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Virginia agency species account describes flathead catfish as an established large-river sportfish.
evidence.observedEffect: Confirms intentional hook-and-line targeting in the region.
evidence.limitations: Does not support environmental bite rules.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Floodplain lake, side channel and main-channel habitats in the lower Mississippi River.
evidence.observedEffect: Feeding ecology and energetic relationships varied among habitat types.
evidence.limitations: Habitat occupancy and prey availability co-vary; no portable bite multiplier.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Telemetry across seasons in the lower St. Joseph River.
evidence.observedEffect: Home range and movement were greatest during warm seasons and minimal in winter.
evidence.limitations: Movement is not feeding or catchability; colder northern system.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Seasonal diel telemetry in the lower St. Joseph River.
evidence.observedEffect: Diel movement varied by season and was often greater at night during warmer periods.
evidence.limitations: No feeding or hook-and-line endpoint; cannot justify a generic nighttime bonus.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Two annual cycles in the lower Missouri River.
evidence.observedEffect: Tributary use and movement increased during putative spawning periods and differed between years; flood conditions may have influenced access.
evidence.limitations: No feeding/catchability measurement and no isolated discharge threshold.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Broad source search for direct species-specific pressure, front, moon, wind or cloud-cover experiments.
evidence.observedEffect: No qualifying direct feeding or hook-and-line evidence was verified.
evidence.limitations: Absence of evidence is not proof of no effect; it supports zero weight.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Juvenile laboratory trials across 3-32 C.
