evidence.observedEffect: Maximum daily consumption increased with temperature, was significantly higher at 19 C than at colder temperatures, and remained elevated through 32 C.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Maximum daily consumption and metabolic demand
evidence.novaApplicability: mechanistically direct but juvenile and nonfield
evidence.limitations: No adult field validation; only exact tested conditions are portable.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Same juvenile laboratory temperature series.
evidence.observedEffect: Fish rarely ate below 15 C, most stopped feeding at 11 C, and none consumed food at 7 C or below.
evidence.limitations: Juvenile laboratory fish; acclimation, prey and exposure duration require full-text confirmation before production calibration.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Reward-tagged flathead catfish in 12 size groups beginning at 381 mm TL.
evidence.observedEffect: Exploitation was highly variable among sizes and reaches rather than forming one consistent size-response curve.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Reported harvest and release corrected for nonreporting
evidence.novaApplicability: direct catchability endpoint but weak portability
evidence.limitations: Angler selectivity, gear, regulations and local abundance confound intrinsic vulnerability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Gear-specific exploitation in the Missouri agency final report associated with the Winders study.
evidence.observedEffect: Rod/reel, trotline, bank-pole and other methods produced different reported exploitation contributions.
evidence.limitations: Gear use and effort were not standardized as a feeding experiment.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 766 flathead catfish captured at more than 1,500 sites; 731 stomachs examined.
evidence.observedEffect: Virginia tidal-river fish were piscine specialists feeding heavily on gizzard shad, white perch, and Alosa species.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Diet composition, trophic level and distribution
evidence.populationLocation: James, Pamunkey, and Mattaponi rivers, Virginia
evidence.limitations: Diet composition does not establish feeding rate, tide, temperature or catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Flathead catfish across size classes in Virginia tidal rivers.
evidence.observedEffect: Dominant fish prey varied among size classes; larger fish remained strongly piscivorous.
evidence.limitations: Size-related diet is not size-related hook vulnerability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Susquehanna River basin diet study detected 47 prey species; crayfish occurred in more than 34% of diets across size classes and fish consumption increased with predator size.
evidence.observedEffect: Flathead catfish showed opportunistic, length-driven diet shifts shaped by regional prey assemblages.
evidence.limitations: Diet occurrence does not quantify feeding intensity or catchability; basin differs from tidal Virginia.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 629 fish sampled across years including a record-flood year.
evidence.observedEffect: Stomach fullness and fish condition differed among flow years, indicating that extreme flow can alter diet and energetic context.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Stomach fullness, diet composition and condition
evidence.novaApplicability: direct feeding context but insufficient portable direction without full text
evidence.limitations: Year, prey community, temperature and sampling differences confound causal flow effects; exact flow thresholds were not verified.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Age-0 fish observed at 5 deg C versus 10, 15, and 20 deg C
evidence.observedEffect: Little feeding activity occurred at 5 deg C; feeding acts increased significantly with temperature at warmer treatments.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Observed feeding acts in controlled temperature treatments
evidence.lifeStage: age-0 fish, approximately 6 g in consumption estimate
evidence.novaApplicability: low-to-moderate for NOVA adult/field transfer; direct endpoint is strong
evidence.limitations: Age-0 laboratory fish and artificial/controlled feeding conditions; not an adult catchability threshold and not a universal cessation point.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Populations near the northwestern native-range edge
evidence.observedEffect: Survival, reproduction, and recruitment were evaluated under cold-climate conditions.
evidence.limitations: Demography and range persistence are not feeding/catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Broad search of intentional angling, vulnerability, bait/lure, pressure, and depletion
evidence.observedEffect: No qualifying intentional hook-and-line catchability experiment was found; gizzard shad functions primarily as forage rather than a NOVA rod-and-reel target.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Evidence absence and independent targetability assessment
evidence.limitations: Other capture methods and rare incidental catches do not establish targetable recreational catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Filter-feeding and particle-capture mechanics investigated in controlled work
evidence.observedEffect: Specialized feeding mechanics support plankton/detritus ecology.
evidence.novaApplicability: low for environmental scoring; useful guide context
evidence.limitations: Full dissertation and exact result pages were not inspected; no quantitative score claim is taken from it.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 10, 15, and 20 deg C
evidence.observedEffect: Estimated food evacuation times were 8.5, 4.9, and 4.4 h, respectively.
evidence.limitations: Only three warmer treatment points; does not establish an optimum or smooth response curve.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Natural detritus diet modeled for a 6-g age-0 fish under study conditions
evidence.observedEffect: Estimated consumption was 3.2-7.7% of wet body weight per day.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Daily ration estimate derived from evacuation and field diet assumptions
evidence.novaApplicability: low transfer to adult fish or NOVA waterbodies
evidence.limitations: Size-, diet-, and study-specific calibration candidate only; not a universal daily intake value.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Small (5-9 mm), medium (10-19 mm), and large (20-29 mm) larvae/early juveniles in two Missouri reservoirs
evidence.observedEffect: Feeding incidence and, to a lesser degree, gut fullness of small and medium fish usually increased with food abundance, but correlations were weak.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Feeding incidence, gut fullness, zooplankton/phytoplankton abundance
evidence.lifeStage: larval and early juvenile age-0 fish
evidence.novaApplicability: low-to-moderate: reservoir age-0 forage ecology, not adult NOVA catchability
evidence.limitations: Weak and inconsistent relationships; site effects differed between reservoirs.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Secchi depth and water temperature across reservoir samples and three size groups
evidence.observedEffect: Feeding incidence and mean gut fullness were not usually correlated with Secchi depth or temperature for any length group.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Field feeding incidence and gut fullness correlations
evidence.evidenceType: field observational study with null findings
evidence.novaApplicability: moderate for rejecting simplistic field clarity/temperature rules
evidence.limitations: Observational ranges and sampling design may lack power; does not contradict the controlled laboratory temperature experiment because endpoints/conditions differ.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 5-9, 10-19, and 20-29 mm total length groups
evidence.observedEffect: Feeding success increased with fish size; diets shifted from copepod nauplii/cyclopoids toward rotifers and phytoplankton as fish grew.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Feeding incidence, gut fullness, diet, and prey size
evidence.lifeStage: larval and early juvenile age-0 fish
evidence.limitations: Ontogenetic effect is not an adult bite modifier and should not be extrapolated beyond age-0 sizes.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Cage temperatures above and below 8 deg C; laboratory treatments of 1, 2, and 4 deg C
evidence.observedEffect: Cage mortality was low above 8 deg C and exceeded 75% as temperature fell below 8 deg C; laboratory mortality rose after 4 deg C and was greatest at 1-2 deg C.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Survival, dry weight, visceral-somatic index, size-dependent mortality
evidence.populationLocation: Oneida Lake, New York, and laboratory
evidence.evidenceType: field cage plus laboratory stress experiment
evidence.limitations: Survival/cold acclimation endpoint, not feeding or hook-and-line catchability. Do not use 8 deg C as a bite threshold.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Within the cold-temperature experiments and winter field collections
evidence.observedEffect: Smaller fish died faster in a winter-temperature treatment; field mean size increased through winter.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Length-dependent mortality and field size distribution
evidence.limitations: Survival selection is not feeding activity.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Variation in gizzard-shad biomass in an Ohio reservoir
evidence.observedEffect: Diet contribution and ecosystem effects shifted with population biomass, indicating density-dependent reliance on zooplankton versus detrital resources.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Diet composition, growth, and food-web response
evidence.limitations: Biomass is not a real-time BiteMap weather input; diet shift does not directly predict hook-and-line catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Virginia native and introduced range.
evidence.observedEffect: Green sunfish occur in Virginia and can be intentionally caught, but they are often a secondary target and local abundance is variable.
evidence.novaApplicability: High regional applicability for guide status
evidence.limitations: Targetability does not prove a predictive environmental rule.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Laboratory breeding and culture conditions.
evidence.observedEffect: Green sunfish could be bred and cultured under controlled conditions, documenting reproductive flexibility.
evidence.limitations: Culture conditions are not natural-water feeding or catchability evidence.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Bull Shoals shoreline centrarchid sampling.
evidence.observedEffect: Green sunfish consumed a mixed diet including substantial crayfish volume in the cited shoreline study.
evidence.limitations: Original full text was not recovered in this run; claim retained only at synthesis level.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Range-wide compiled evidence.
evidence.observedEffect: The synthesis describes broad habitat, diet, and invasion traits but provides no validated short-term bite function.
evidence.limitations: Secondary synthesis cannot replace endpoint-specific primary research.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Environmental variables separated from abundance, effort, gear, and access.
evidence.observedEffect: No qualifying green-sunfish study directly estimated species-specific environmental effects on hook-and-line catchability.
evidence.limitations: Lack of direct research does not mean the fish cannot be intentionally targeted.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Barometric pressure, fronts, wind, rainfall, cloud cover, and moon phase.
evidence.observedEffect: No qualifying green-sunfish feeding or angling study isolated these variables.
evidence.limitations: Do not substitute centrarchid folklore or related-species evidence.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: HSI synthesis across life stages.
evidence.observedEffect: Green sunfish were modeled as habitat generalists favoring warm, low-gradient habitats with cover; suitability variables describe carrying capacity rather than bite probability.
evidence.limitations: Model assumptions combine literature, expert judgment, and surrogate information.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: HSI oxygen component.
evidence.observedEffect: The report explicitly relied partly on bluegill or generalized centrarchid information because green-sunfish-specific oxygen data were limited.
evidence.novaApplicability: Not direct evidence for green sunfish scoring
evidence.limitations: Related-species surrogate evidence cannot support a green-sunfish score rule.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Moderate turbidity range in the HSI synthesis, approximately 25-100 JTU.
evidence.observedEffect: The synthesis reported an abundance association with moderate turbidity, but also warned that cause and effect were not established.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Field abundance correlations summarized in HSI
evidence.limitations: JTU is not directly interchangeable with NTU; abundance is not feeding or catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Juveniles assigned combinations of food ration and water temperature.
evidence.observedEffect: Food ration and temperature were similarly important to juvenile growth; abundant food at a suboptimal temperature could produce growth similar to scarce food near an optimum.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Juvenile growth under controlled ration-temperature treatments
evidence.limitations: Growth does not establish an adult feeding optimum or hook-and-line response.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Clear, 4-6 JTU, and 14-16 JTU aquaria for 30 days.
evidence.observedEffect: Juvenile green-sunfish activity declined numerically with turbidity, but the reported reduction was not statistically significant.
evidence.novaApplicability: Direct null/weak activity evidence, not feeding
evidence.limitations: Small aquaria, juvenile stage, and JTU units limit transfer.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Repeated electroshocking in a warmwater stream study.
evidence.observedEffect: Green sunfish showed no significant effect on measured growth or movement in the reported comparisons.
evidence.limitations: Electrofishing disturbance is not angling pressure or ordinary weather.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Green sunfish and bluegill coexistence experiments/observations.
evidence.observedEffect: Habitat use shifted in response to competition, demonstrating that occupancy is conditional on community composition.
evidence.limitations: Habitat shift is not feeding or hook-and-line catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Controlled warm and cool acclimation treatments.
evidence.observedEffect: Whole-organism thermal thresholds and mitochondrial bioenergetics changed rapidly with acclimation.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Critical thermal limits and mitochondrial performance
evidence.novaApplicability: Context only; supports avoiding fixed universal thresholds
evidence.limitations: Preprint status and physiological endpoints preclude bite scoring.

evidence.variable: Regional habitat, diel feeding context, and reproduction
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Virginia; spawning typically March-May; low-light periods described as especially active feeding periods
evidence.observedEffect: Agency account describes use of slow or calm water and submerged cover, feeding throughout the day with stronger low-light feeding, and spring nesting with male brood guarding.
evidence.limitations: Agency synthesis does not quantify catchability, underwater light, spawning temperature, or waterbody-specific timing.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Lower Neuse River; discharge below versus above 85 m3/s, with a steep CPUE change between 60 and 100 m3/s
evidence.observedEffect: Boat-electrofishing CPUE was usually lower above 85 m3/s and frequently higher below it.
evidence.populationLocation: Lower Neuse River tributaries, North Carolina
evidence.novaApplicability: Qualitative coastal-river context only; numerical threshold is not portable
evidence.limitations: Electrofishing CPUE confounds abundance, fish relocation, conductivity, visibility, inundated habitat, boat access, and gear efficiency. It is not hook-and-line catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 50 NTU
evidence.observedEffect: Maryland DNR's synthesis reports that foraging by age-1 largemouth bass was reduced by at least 33% at 50 NTU.
evidence.populationLocation: Primary experiment synthesized in a Chesapeake tidal-bass plan
evidence.novaApplicability: Relevant to regional juveniles; uncertain for adult lure capture

sourceLocator.section: Population structure and dynamics - juvenile growth and foraging

evidence.limitations: Secondary reporting of the primary experiment. Does not establish an adult optimum, a beneficial moderate-turbidity band, or hook-and-line catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: High salinity above 5 ppt or absence of submerged cover following displacement
evidence.observedEffect: Maryland DNR's synthesis reports movement away from release areas; freshwater and brackish-adapted adults differ in salinity tolerance and condition.
evidence.populationLocation: Chesapeake and other tidal populations synthesized by Maryland DNR
evidence.novaApplicability: Relevant to lower tidal Potomac and Chesapeake tributaries
evidence.limitations: This is not a universal salinity maximum, feeding threshold, or direct catchability effect. Local acclimation and genetics matter.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 38 radio-tagged adults; four migratory fish crossed the upper Chesapeake Bay during spring
evidence.observedEffect: The four migrants had a mean home range of 2,140 ha and returned to the Northeast River area two to three months later; migration was suspected to be spawning-related.
evidence.novaApplicability: High regional relevance to tidal Chesapeake tributaries
evidence.limitations: Only four fish showed this migration. No ebb/flood comparison, current-speed effect, feeding rate, or hook-and-line catchability was measured.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Laboratory acclimation at 25.0, 14.0, and 7.5-8.5 C; seasonal field observations
evidence.observedEffect: Critical swimming speed was 2.17, 1.69, and 1.17 body lengths per second at the three acclimation temperatures. Early-winter field activity metrics were 63.3%-75.6% below summer values.
evidence.populationLocation: Warner Lake and Lake Opinicon, Ontario
evidence.novaApplicability: Strong taxonomic relevance but colder climate than Northern Virginia

sourceLocator.section: Abstract; Results - Direct laboratory and field comparisons; Swim-tunnel experiments

evidence.limitations: Movement and swimming performance are not feeding or hook-and-line catchability. The paper uses 7.5 C in the abstract but 8.5 C for the early-spring swim-tunnel group in the results.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Five fish acclimated to 22 C and acutely tested at 15, 20, 25, and 30 C
evidence.observedEffect: Mean fastest times to peak gape were 23.3, 22.4, 18.2, and 22.0 ms, respectively; the fastest mouth-opening kinematics occurred at 25 C.
evidence.populationLocation: Laboratory population; lineage not genetically verified
evidence.novaApplicability: Mechanistically relevant but weak as a field forecast threshold
evidence.limitations: Only five fish; acute exposure; mouth-opening speed is not appetite, prey consumption, or angling catchability. It cannot establish a 77 F bite optimum.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 35 C (95 F) for 28 days
evidence.observedEffect: All size groups consumed less than 0.21% of body weight per day and showed little biologically meaningful growth; authors interpreted prolonged exposure as thermal stress.
evidence.populationLocation: Captive northern largemouth bass in recirculating tanks
evidence.lifeStage: 80 g, 105 g, and 137 g size classes
evidence.novaApplicability: Lineage relevant, but aquaculture conditions and commercial feed differ from wild fish
evidence.limitations: Only the abstract was accessible. The study does not establish when feeding first declines, a field catchability threshold, or a cooler control within the reviewed text.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Winter habitat below approximately 2.0 mg/L; juvenile laboratory exposures at 1.99 and 1.42 mg/L at 5 C
evidence.observedEffect: Telemetered adults avoided water below about 2.0 mg/L. Juveniles began yawning and vertical movement at 1.99 mg/L, with stronger responses at 1.42 mg/L.
evidence.populationLocation: Warner Lake, Ontario, plus laboratory experiments
evidence.lifeStage: Adults in field; juveniles in laboratory
evidence.novaApplicability: Strong for winter avoidance; warm-season transfer is uncertain
evidence.limitations: Not a universal feeding-cessation threshold. Fish sometimes used intermediate oxygen and briefly entered lower-oxygen water; temperature and other habitat variables interacted.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Toronto Harbour year-round; dawn, day, dusk, and night
evidence.observedEffect: Mean acceleration was lower in winter (0.172 m/s2) and fall (0.277 m/s2) than spring (0.572 m/s2) and summer (0.642 m/s2). Dawn acceleration was 0.521 m/s2 and night was 0.278 m/s2.
evidence.novaApplicability: Taxonomically relevant but colder, urban Great Lakes setting
evidence.limitations: Acceleration averaged over 20-minute intervals primarily reflects sustained movement or transit and may miss short feeding bursts. It is not angling catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Six complete lunar cycles across winter, spring, and summer
evidence.observedEffect: Lunar phase related to depth or movement in some cycles, but patterns were inconsistent across the year and not repeatable. Authors concluded solunar tables may have little predictive value for peak fishing time.
evidence.novaApplicability: Moderate biological applicability; no direct angling test
evidence.limitations: No hook-and-line catchability outcome. Moon phase is an incomplete proxy for actual underwater illumination and can be confounded with season.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Nesting males guarding newly spawned eggs; six-cast experimental angling trials
evidence.observedEffect: 54% of nesting male largemouth bass were hooked; vulnerability was associated with brood size and aggressive brood defense.
evidence.novaApplicability: Strong mechanism; Virginia timing must be determined regionally
evidence.limitations: Only the abstract was accessible. The response is territorial aggression and nest defense, not increased feeding; it does not apply to females or all spawning fish.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Two May-October fishing seasons in six small impoundments, including a two-month closure
evidence.observedEffect: Catch rate and catchability declined with sustained effort, increased after the closure, and then declined again; results supported learned angler avoidance.
evidence.novaApplicability: Strong qualitative applicability to pressured ponds and reservoirs
evidence.limitations: Only the abstract was accessible. Magnitude depends on effort, lures, prior capture, population structure, and waterbody openness.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Four to five cobbles separated by less than 1 m; summer, autumn, spring
evidence.observedEffect: Foraging intensity was not correlated with benthic macroinvertebrate biomass per cobble in any season.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Observed bites per cobble and macroinvertebrate biomass
evidence.limitations: Important null finding: prey density on a single cobble did not predict bite intensity.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 783 juveniles and 857 adults in a Michigan stream
evidence.observedEffect: Juveniles and adults used habitat differently.
evidence.limitations: Habitat occupancy is not feeding/catchability; exact size-habitat effects require full text.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Mink River sympatry
evidence.observedEffect: Longnose and blacknose dace segregated ecologically in stream habitat.
evidence.limitations: Distant geography and habitat endpoint only.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Riverine and lacustrine habitat variables
evidence.observedEffect: The agency report models physical habitat suitability for longnose dace.
evidence.limitations: HSI values predict habitat suitability, not feeding motivation or angler catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Susquehanna tributary stock
evidence.observedEffect: Embryo-to-juvenile development was described for longnose and blacknose dace.
evidence.limitations: Early-life development is not an adult feeding/catchability endpoint.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Broad variable-specific search
evidence.observedEffect: No direct hook-and-line catchability experiment and no defensible oxygen, pressure, front, moon, stocking, or angling-pressure score were found.
evidence.limitations: Niche microfishing exists conceptually, but the species is not a mainstream target and absence of research is not proof of no effect.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Foraging patches less than 5 m diameter
evidence.observedEffect: In summer, when prey were patchily distributed, dace used cobbles with significantly higher macroinvertebrate biomass than nearby physically similar random cobbles; no such selection occurred in autumn or spring when prey were homogeneous.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Direct foraging-patch selection and prey biomass
evidence.limitations: Conditional on local summer prey patchiness and comparable stream habitat; not a smooth prey-response curve.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Erosional reaches 11-19 m long
evidence.observedEffect: Among physically suitable reaches, prey biomass correlated positively with dace density in all seasons; prey patchiness explained most among-reach abundance variation.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Fish density and prey biomass by reach
evidence.limitations: Fish abundance/habitat occupancy, not per-fish feeding rate or catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Depositional low-current sand/silt/debris versus erosional cobble/boulder high-current reaches
evidence.observedEffect: Dace avoided depositional habitats even where food was abundant; no adult dace were observed in one high-food depositional reach.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Habitat selection with food availability measured
evidence.limitations: Strong location context but still not a direct catchability multiplier.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Daylight snorkeling in summer/autumn 1996 and spring 1997
evidence.observedEffect: Coweeta longnose dace were regularly observed as active daytime foragers; dietary work in that system supported diurnal feeding.
evidence.limitations: System-specific; conflicts with Alberta nocturnal evidence.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Southern Alberta stream population
evidence.observedEffect: Foraging was constrained to nighttime in the reviewed Alberta population.
evidence.limitations: Geographically distant and contradicted by Coweeta observations; no universal night bonus is defensible.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Different light intensities
evidence.observedEffect: Foraging behavior changed with light intensity, demonstrating plasticity.
evidence.limitations: Exact light levels and response magnitudes were not extracted from full text; unavailable for scoring.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Stream stomach-content study
evidence.observedEffect: Longnose dace consumed benthic prey; diet composition supports benthic presentation.
evidence.limitations: No environmental feeding-rate response extracted.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Blacknose versus longnose dace
evidence.observedEffect: The two dace species differed in food habits, reinforcing species-specific prey/presentation context.
evidence.limitations: No portable predictor extracted without full text.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Moving prey presented under darkness/non-visual conditions
evidence.observedEffect: Mottled sculpin could detect and attack moving prey without relying on vision.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Prey-location and attack behavior under non-visual conditions
evidence.novaApplicability: moderate: sensory mechanism is relevant, but exact transfer to NOVA streams is uncertain
evidence.limitations: The accessible record supports non-visual prey detection, not a higher nocturnal feeding rate or hook-and-line catchability. Exact trial conditions require full-text reinspection.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Broad search across angling, vulnerability, gear, pressure, depletion, and learning themes
evidence.observedEffect: No qualifying direct hook-and-line catchability experiment was located.
evidence.populationLocation: NOVA-priority and broader North American literature

sourceLocator.section: Agency profile plus documented search audit

evidence.limitations: Absence of evidence is not evidence that the species cannot be caught intentionally.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Species-specific direct feeding/catchability search
evidence.observedEffect: No portable DO threshold or temperature-oxygen feeding interaction was found.
evidence.novaApplicability: high relevance as a model gap
evidence.limitations: Physiological tolerance literature must not be substituted for feeding response.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Species is a small benthic stream fish and not a common intentional hook-and-line target in the NOVA product context
evidence.observedEffect: Scientific feeding studies exist, but recreational targeting and catchability evidence are inadequate for a production bite score.
evidence.limitations: Guide-only status does not imply ecological unimportance or absolute uncatchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Spring, summer, and autumn samples during 2021-2022 in a regulated oligotrophic high-elevation river
evidence.observedEffect: Autumn had the highest frequency of empty stomachs and lower stomach fullness when benthic prey biomass was lowest.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Stomach contents, stomach fullness index, empty-stomach frequency, benthic prey biomass, and stable isotopes
evidence.lifeStage: mixed sizes of wild mottled sculpin
evidence.novaApplicability: low-to-moderate: direct feeding endpoint but distant regulated high-elevation system
evidence.limitations: Season, prey biomass, regulated flow, temperature, and competition covary. This cannot justify a universal autumn or monthly penalty.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Season-specific electivity estimates in 2021-2022
evidence.observedEffect: Electivity varied by season and prey taxon; some amphipod, dipteran, and ephemeropteran prey were positively selected in particular samples.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Stomach prey composition relative to benthic availability
evidence.novaApplicability: low-to-moderate: useful Fish Guide context; prey community differs from NOVA
evidence.limitations: Selection was not stable across all seasons/years and does not establish lure-specific or universal prey rules.

evidence.variable: current velocity, depth, and substrate position
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Underwater observations in Pennsylvania streams
evidence.observedEffect: Mottled sculpin occurred in shallower, faster habitats than available and were most often beneath substrate.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Focal depth, water velocity, substrate size, and position
evidence.novaApplicability: moderate-to-high geographic relevance for Mid-Atlantic streams
evidence.limitations: Habitat occupancy was measured, not feeding or angling catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Three-year mark-recapture and snorkeling study; juveniles <48 mm SL, adults 49-64 and >65 mm SL
evidence.observedEffect: Adults had restricted, strongly territorial home ranges with <10% overlap; juveniles overlapped more and occupied less-stable margins.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Movement, home range, overlap, territory abandonment, substrate stability
evidence.novaApplicability: moderate: southern Appalachian stream is regionally closer than western studies
evidence.limitations: Territoriality and space use may affect location, but feeding rate and catchability were not measured.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Seasonal flow metrics and territory abandonment in the same stream study
evidence.observedEffect: Adult territorial behavior was more closely related to density of large adults than to flow variability or microhabitat stability.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Home-range behavior, abandonment, flow metrics, population age structure
evidence.evidenceType: field movement study with null/relative findings
evidence.limitations: Null/relative movement finding cannot be converted to a flow-bite rule.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Mark-recapture evaluation in a Michigan stream
evidence.observedEffect: Most fish were relatively sedentary, but a nontrivial minority moved farther than a strict restricted-movement assumption would predict.
evidence.limitations: Movement is not feeding; abstract-only access limits exact distance transcription here.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Comparative stomach-content observations with salmonids
evidence.observedEffect: Mottled sculpin consumed benthic animal prey and overlapped with salmonid prey resources.
evidence.limitations: Historical full text was not inspected; diet identity is presentation context, not an environmental response.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: High-hardness-water zinc exposures
evidence.observedEffect: Zinc toxicity thresholds were evaluated for mottled sculpin.
evidence.limitations: Stress and survival are not feeding or catchability; contaminant-specific results are outside routine BiteMap inputs.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: DWR identifies established and stocked fisheries in the James, New, Shenandoah and Tennessee systems.
evidence.observedEffect: Confirms intentional Virginia recreational targeting.
evidence.limitations: Does not establish bite predictors.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 1,092 muskellunge from 34 Wisconsin waters, 226-1,180 mm.
evidence.observedEffect: Food occurred in 34.3% of stomachs; diet was diverse and varied with size and availability.
evidence.limitations: Stomach occurrence is affected by digestion and capture timing.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Acoustic telemetry in a large connecting-river system.
evidence.observedEffect: Seasonal movements crossed jurisdictions and habitats.
evidence.limitations: Movement does not establish feeding or hook vulnerability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Virginia management plan documents low-density trophy fisheries and stocking dependence.
evidence.observedEffect: Supports availability, regulations and population context.
evidence.limitations: Low density affects encounter probability but is not per-fish bite rate.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Baseline archive repeated an agency-style claim that feeding stops near 84 F.
evidence.observedEffect: No original species-specific feeding experiment supporting a universal 84 F cessation threshold was verified.
evidence.limitations: Physiological tolerance and anecdote cannot become an exact bite threshold.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Broad direct-evidence search.
evidence.observedEffect: No robust species-specific pressure/front rule was verified; Escanaba wind-direction effects were tiny and plausibly behavioral/effort confounding.
evidence.limitations: Wind may alter presentation or effort without a direct physiological mechanism.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Escanaba Lake trip records from low (<25 W/m2) to high (>450 W/m2) radiation.
evidence.observedEffect: Modeled trip-success probability declined from about 0.17 at low radiation to about 0.11 at high radiation.
evidence.limitations: All modeled effects were very small; angler behavior and presentation may covary.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Dawn, day and dusk among successful Escanaba Lake trips.
evidence.observedEffect: Positive-trip CPUE was highest at dusk, but only nine successful dusk trips were available.
evidence.limitations: Severe sample-size limitation and no overnight fishing.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 341,959 voluntary catch records from North America, 1970-2013.
evidence.observedEffect: Catch was cyclic with the lunar month; more fish were reported near full and new moons, with a small effect roughly equivalent to about 5% less time per catch.
evidence.limitations: Effort, reporting, trip timing and latitude can confound; mechanism was not demonstrated.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Escanaba Lake moon overhead, underfoot or neither.
evidence.observedEffect: Trip success was somewhat higher near overhead/underfoot, but positive-trip CPUE showed a different ordering.
evidence.limitations: Do not stack lunar phase and moon-position bonuses; effects were very small.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: James River warm-water period, July-August, with water commonly >25 C.
evidence.observedEffect: Few tagged muskellunge were caught during the warm-water window, limiting population-level effects of release mortality.
evidence.novaApplicability: high geographic relevance, but low event count
evidence.limitations: Low catches may reflect angler effort, fish behavior, distribution or gear; no continuous temperature response was established.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 50 angled fish at 19.6-32.6 C; 32 captures above 25 C in experimental ponds.
evidence.observedEffect: Study quantified post-release mortality at elevated temperatures.
evidence.limitations: Mortality and physiological stress are not catchability or feeding.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Live versus artificial bait; guided versus unguided trips.
evidence.observedEffect: Live bait and guided trips had modestly higher predicted success; all effect sizes were very small.
evidence.limitations: Skill, effort and trip selection confound.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Age-0 muskellunge and northern pike offered multiple prey types in laboratory trials.
evidence.observedEffect: Species differed in prey selection and time to consumption.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Prey choice and time to consume prey
evidence.limitations: No environmental predictor and no adult catchability endpoint.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Federal species profile
evidence.observedEffect: Accepted name Hypentelium nigricans; common name Northern Hog Sucker.
evidence.limitations: No predictive endpoint.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Spring 2004-2005 Savannah River spawning aggregations
evidence.observedEffect: Northern hogsucker was the smallest of the four species and reached sexual maturity at age 3.
evidence.limitations: Demography is not feeding or catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 1983-1992 southern Appalachian stream study
evidence.observedEffect: Hydrologic period, season, and fish length were evaluated as microhabitat correlates.
evidence.limitations: Exact hogsucker response not extracted; no feeding endpoint.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: New Jersey Mid-Atlantic species account
evidence.observedEffect: The species occurs in the Mid-Atlantic and is associated with clean, flowing stream habitat; regional conservation status may constrain targeting.
evidence.limitations: Agency synthesis; habitat presence is not feeding or catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 25 radio-tagged fish followed for one year
evidence.observedEffect: Mean daily distance was 425 m in summer versus 276 m in winter.
evidence.limitations: Movement is not feeding or hook-and-line catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Winter/spring versus summer/fall
evidence.observedEffect: Mean home range was 812 m in winter/spring versus 426 m in summer/fall.
evidence.limitations: Home-range size cannot be converted to a bite score.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Hourly records for 17 winter days and 12 summer days
evidence.observedEffect: Fish moved more during the day than at night.
evidence.limitations: The study did not directly measure ingestion, attack rate, or angling catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Winter day: pools/moderate flow; winter night: riffle edges; summer day: runs; summer night: riffle edges
evidence.observedEffect: Habitat shifted by season and diel period.
evidence.limitations: Authors interpreted some daytime use as feeding, but feeding was not measured. Retain only as habitat context.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: High-flow events
evidence.observedEffect: Fish remained in home areas but used flooded riparian areas with lower velocities.
evidence.limitations: Floodplain use is location/refuge behavior, not evidence of increased feeding.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Late February to early March; seven fish
evidence.observedEffect: Mean spawning-related movement was 497 m.
evidence.limitations: Aggregation/migration does not establish feeding or catchability and may reflect reproduction.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Low-water road crossing in an Ozark stream
evidence.observedEffect: Movement was affected by the crossing, demonstrating a connectivity constraint.
evidence.limitations: Barrier movement study; no feeding endpoint and no direct NOVA calibration.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Seven catostomid species sampled in four Iowa rivers in 2009
evidence.observedEffect: Northern hogsucker was included in a stomach-content/gill-raker study, but the accessible abstract did not provide a portable species-specific environmental feeding response.
evidence.limitations: No numerical hogsucker-specific rule extracted from the abstract.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Established Chesapeake/Potomac population managed as invasive harvest target.
evidence.observedEffect: Confirms intentional hook-and-line targeting in the application region.
evidence.limitations: Management goal and harvest encouragement do not establish bite predictors.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Published bioenergetics information used to simulate Chesapeake watershed maximum consumption.
evidence.observedEffect: Model predicted temperature-dependent maximum consumption and large annual prey demand, explicitly representing maximum rather than realized natural feeding.
evidence.novaApplicability: regional context; not observed bite rate
evidence.limitations: Model inputs came from published studies/populations; maximum consumption is not field intake or catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 188.54 +/- 13.80 g fish fed 0, 1, 2, 4% body weight/day or satiation at 28 C.
evidence.observedEffect: Specific growth rate increased with ration; energy allocation and conversion changed with feeding level.
evidence.limitations: Ration was imposed; this does not identify environmental drivers of voluntary feeding.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Newly established Potomac population.
evidence.observedEffect: Growth and reproductive behavior were documented for the local population.
evidence.limitations: No standardized catchability endpoint.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Early invasion years in the Potomac system.
evidence.observedEffect: Catch/relative abundance increased dramatically as the population expanded.
evidence.limitations: Increase reflects abundance, colonization and survey catchability, not individual feeding.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Acute temperature changes after acclimation in laboratory snakehead.
evidence.observedEffect: Respiratory metabolism depended on acclimation and acute temperature.
evidence.novaApplicability: low portability to field bite scoring
evidence.limitations: Metabolism is not feeding or hook-and-line catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Baseline description suggested flexible feeding with frequent low-light activity.
evidence.observedEffect: Direct Potomac evidence instead found daylight/morning feeding and no fresh prey overnight during the sampled season.
evidence.limitations: Season-specific evidence should not become a year-round daylight curve.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 273 fish sampled through 24 h during May-June 2007-2008; fresh prey occurrence by capture time.
evidence.observedEffect: No fresh prey items were found from about 00:30 to 07:30; feeding and movement were greater during daylight and feeding was highest in the morning.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Fresh gut contents and telemetry movement
evidence.evidenceType: in situ field sampling and telemetry
evidence.limitations: Only May-June; electrofishing capture and digestion timing can affect temporal inference.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Feeding observations classified by tidal phase in the same Potomac study.
evidence.observedEffect: Feeding was highest during outgoing tides.
evidence.limitations: Time of day and tide covary; model explained only a small fraction of variation.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Random-forest predictors included time, tide, date, temperature, total length and sex.
evidence.observedEffect: The model explained about 6% of feeding variation; time and tide were more informative than a portable temperature threshold.
evidence.novaApplicability: high local relevance but weak explanatory power
evidence.limitations: Do not infer a temperature curve from variable importance.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: May-June sampling across onset of spawning.
evidence.observedEffect: Empty stomach frequency increased near the end of May as spawning began.
evidence.limitations: Reduced feeding does not rule out defensive or territorial strikes.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Seasonal meso- and microhabitat selection in the Potomac system.
evidence.observedEffect: Fish selected shallow, vegetated and low-velocity habitats with seasonal variation.
evidence.limitations: Occupancy is not feeding or catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Tagged fish in the Potomac catchment across seasons.
evidence.observedEffect: Movement, dispersal and home range varied seasonally and among individuals.
evidence.limitations: Movement does not establish appetite or a bite multiplier.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Radio telemetry and survey observations in tidal Potomac tributaries.
evidence.observedEffect: Fish occupied tributaries and tidal habitats and showed movement among locations.
evidence.limitations: No direct feeding endpoint.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Lower Potomac stomach contents compared with largemouth bass, smallmouth bass and channel catfish.
evidence.observedEffect: Northern snakehead consumed diverse fishes and other prey; diet overlapped with co-occurring predators.
evidence.limitations: Diet occurrence does not quantify day-specific catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Virginia ponds, lakes, and slow waters.
evidence.observedEffect: Pumpkinseed are present and intentionally catchable in Virginia, although local abundance and angler targeting vary.
evidence.limitations: Agency account is not direct catchability experimentation.

evidence.variable: Sustained angling removal and population response
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Repeated removal through angling in ten artificial lakes.
evidence.observedEffect: Angling removal altered population size structure, maximum mass, and juvenile growth patterns over time.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Population characteristics and juvenile growth under removal
evidence.limitations: Long-term removal effects do not yield a short-term hook-avoidance or bite-decay function.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 2,435 pumpkinseed stomachs across age groups and seasons.
evidence.observedEffect: Diet and habitat use changed with size and age; younger and older fish exploited different prey and spaces.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Stomach contents and habitat by age group
evidence.limitations: No real-time environmental catchability function.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Introduced European populations exposed to warmer conditions.
evidence.observedEffect: Elevated temperature advanced spawning timing.
evidence.limitations: Introduced populations and climate differ; earlier spawning is not a feeding optimum.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Warm-water introduced population comparisons.
evidence.observedEffect: Temperature affected growth, maturation, and other life-history traits.
evidence.limitations: Growth and life history are not bite endpoints.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Shy-bold continuum measured in juvenile pumpkinseed.
evidence.observedEffect: Behavioral type covaried with ecological traits including diet and risk exposure.
evidence.limitations: No operational weather or habitat trigger; phenotype effects may be plastic.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Parental males observed across a nesting season.
evidence.observedEffect: Larger and older males nested earlier; later nests were dominated by younger/smaller males.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Nest timing, male size, and age
evidence.limitations: Nesting timing is not feeding or catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Four hook types used for bluegill and pumpkinseed angling.
evidence.observedEffect: Hook type influenced injury patterns and capture outcomes; findings inform catch-and-release handling.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Capture efficiency, injury, and short-term mortality
evidence.novaApplicability: Fish Guide relevance, not environmental score
evidence.limitations: Gear-specific and not a weather/environmental predictor.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Barometric pressure, fronts, wind, rainfall, cloud cover, and natural moon phase.
evidence.observedEffect: No qualifying pumpkinseed study isolated these variables for feeding or hook-and-line catchability.
evidence.limitations: Artificial or categorical light studies cannot be translated into solunar weights.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Whole-diel stomach sampling during the breeding season.
evidence.observedEffect: Parental males had lower total food weight than females; cuckolder males did not show the same reduction.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Stomach content mass by reproductive tactic and sex
evidence.lifeStage: Adult parental males, cuckolder males, and females
evidence.limitations: Introduced European population; do not apply to all adults or all spawning periods.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Breeding-season stomach samples.
evidence.observedEffect: Parental males contained lower numbers and weight of chironomids than comparison groups.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Prey number and mass by taxon
evidence.limitations: Reduced chironomids may reflect nest-site foraging constraints rather than overall appetite alone.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Repeated sampling across a 24-hour cycle.
evidence.observedEffect: Stomach fullness peaked near dawn and dusk, most clearly in parental males.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Stomach fullness across time of day
evidence.novaApplicability: Potential context; not a universal hourly bite curve
evidence.limitations: Single reproductive season and population; light, prey, and temperature covary.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Breeding-season stomach contents.
evidence.observedEffect: Parental males were more likely to contain conspecific eggs, showing reproductive-state-specific prey use.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Occurrence of conspecific eggs in stomachs
evidence.limitations: May include filial cannibalism or egg removal; not an angling predictor.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Nesting and nonnesting pumpkinseed sampled at dawn and dusk.
evidence.observedEffect: Nesting reduced prey quantity and diversity relative to nonnesting fish.
evidence.limitations: Abstract-level access; exact magnitude and covariates require full-text recheck.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Active and passive angling during bright, low-light, and dark periods.
evidence.observedEffect: Pumpkinseed caught in dark or low light were more often deeply or foul hooked than those caught in bright conditions.
evidence.novaApplicability: Direct angling handling evidence; limited as bite-score input
evidence.limitations: Few pumpkinseed were caught at night; result concerns injury risk, not higher catch probability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Active lure presentation versus passive bait presentation.
evidence.observedEffect: Passive angling produced deeper hooking for the study fishes, including pumpkinseed.
evidence.limitations: Gear effect, not environmental bite scoring.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Nighttime angling periods in the diel study.
evidence.observedEffect: Few pumpkinseed were captured at night, preventing a strong night catch-rate conclusion.
evidence.novaApplicability: Supports rejection of a generic night bonus
evidence.limitations: Sampling design targeted hooking-depth questions, not standardized population catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Virginia wild rainbow-trout populations and fisheries described in the state management plan.
evidence.observedEffect: Confirms intentional regional targeting and distinguishes wild from stocked management.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Distribution, management status, habitat and life history
evidence.novaApplicability: high for targetability; low for bite prediction
evidence.limitations: Natural-history statements do not establish bite optima.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Turbidity up to 160 NTU; benthic chironomids and mayfly prey; total darkness included.
evidence.observedEffect: Turbidity altered size selection for some prey, and chironomids were consumed in darkness.
evidence.limitations: Prey-specific and juvenile; natural light and lure detection were not measured.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Wild rainbow trout 87-185 mm exposed to suspended sediment in artificial channels.
evidence.observedEffect: Reactive distance and pursuit behavior changed with turbidity.
evidence.novaApplicability: contextual mechanism, not consumption or angling
evidence.limitations: A shorter reactive distance does not uniquely predict catch rate; prey density and encounter distance matter.

evidence.variable: turbidity, temperature, prey availability and piscivory
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Colorado River field observations spanning broad suspended-sediment conditions.
evidence.observedEffect: Piscivory varied with turbidity, temperature, and fish-prey availability; higher turbidity did not imply a simple feeding penalty.
evidence.novaApplicability: low-to-moderate transfer due ecosystem and diet differences
evidence.limitations: Correlated covariates, extreme sediment regime, and piscivorous subset prevent a portable single-variable rule.

evidence.variable: prey availability, hunger and prey size
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Controlled encounters varying hunger, prey density, and prey size.
evidence.observedEffect: Attack and consumption depended on energetic state and prey field.
evidence.limitations: Does not yield a public environmental API threshold; prey abundance is rarely observed directly.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Bait angling of sympatric salmonids in natural Japanese streams.
evidence.observedEffect: Vulnerability and size selectivity differed among salmonid species.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Hook-and-line captures by species and size
evidence.novaApplicability: supports population/species context but limited geographic transfer
evidence.limitations: Different fish community, fishing style, and population histories; exact ranking should not be generalized without local validation.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Repeated catch-and-release angling in an experimental rainbow-trout fishery.
evidence.observedEffect: Study evaluated growth and survival consequences rather than a short-term bite-probability function.
evidence.limitations: No direct same-day or next-day recapture rule was isolated for NOVA waters.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 5,689 interviews on 14 Virginia put-and-take waters; species were pooled.
evidence.observedEffect: Catch was fastest on stocking day; both catch rate and effort varied with time after stocking, site, and month.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Angler catch per hour and effort
evidence.novaApplicability: high for stocked Virginia waters but not species-specific
evidence.limitations: Rainbow, brown, and brook trout were not separated; effort, access, harvest, and site are confounders.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Day after through 16-30 days after stocking on Virginia put-and-take waters.
evidence.observedEffect: After the initial stocking-day peak, average catch rates stayed near 1 trout per angler-hour and were statistically similar across post-stocking intervals for up to a month.
evidence.novaApplicability: high for rejecting a simple decay rule; species transfer limited
evidence.limitations: Does not prove no local depletion; species were pooled and stockings sometimes overlapped.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Stocked rainbow trout >300 mm compared with fish <260 mm in one Adirondack river.
evidence.observedEffect: Larger rainbow trout were caught at higher rates.
evidence.populationLocation: West Branch Sacandaga River, New York
evidence.novaApplicability: moderate ecological similarity but not Mid-Atlantic
evidence.limitations: Only two reported size groups; stocking, visibility, gear, and refuge use may contribute.

evidence.variable: extreme heat, thermal refuge and catchability
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Summer water temperatures exceeded 20 C in a thermally marginal stocked river with cool refuges.
evidence.observedEffect: High temperature did not reduce observed catch rates because fish concentrated in cool refuges; this was especially noted for brook trout.
evidence.novaApplicability: contextual; warns against treating thermal stress as automatic low catchability
evidence.limitations: Catch concentration is not increased feeding; exact refuge geometry and stocked status limit transfer.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 42 days at 14 C; approximately 7.9 versus 4.5 mg O2/L; isogenic cultured rainbow trout fed ad libitum.
evidence.observedEffect: Hypoxia reduced feed intake by about 6% and growth by about 8%.
evidence.novaApplicability: mechanistically relevant, but chronic aquaculture exposure is not a field bite curve
evidence.limitations: One line, diet treatments, chronic exposure, and constant temperature; do not interpolate a universal oxygen curve.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Same 42-day 14 C comparison of 7.9 and 4.5 mg O2/L.
evidence.observedEffect: Hypoxia reduced oxygen consumption and altered metabolic/osmoregulatory responses.
evidence.limitations: Physiology is not catchability and may overlap the feed-intake rule.

evidence.variable: dissolved oxygen and maximal feed intake
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Normoxic versus reduced-oxygen cultured rainbow trout in a feeding trial.
evidence.observedEffect: Lower oxygen reduced maximal voluntary feed intake, while utilization efficiency was not the primary limiting response.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Maximum feed intake and nutrient utilization
evidence.limitations: Abstract-level evidence; exact transfer to wild fish, acclimation state, and short exposures is unresolved.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Juveniles offered Daphnia and benthic prey at turbidity up to 160 NTU in laboratory tanks.
evidence.observedEffect: Overall feeding rate was not reduced across the tested turbidity range.
evidence.novaApplicability: limited by life stage and artificial prey field
evidence.limitations: Cannot establish adult angling response or conditions beyond 160 NTU.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Virginia and adjoining Mid-Atlantic waters.
evidence.observedEffect: Agency and management records identify redbreast sunfish as an established, intentionally fished river and stream panfish.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Regional occurrence, fishing use, and management context
evidence.novaApplicability: High regional applicability; not a short-term bite predictor
evidence.limitations: Agency synthesis does not isolate intrinsic catchability from abundance or angler effort.

evidence.variable: Population variation in growth and survival
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 5,664 bluegill and redbreast sunfish from 13 Georgia river sections.
evidence.observedEffect: Growth and annual survival varied substantially among river sections; redbreast survival estimates ranged broadly.
evidence.limitations: No feeding or angling endpoint was measured.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Nesting and nonnesting redbreast sunfish sampled at dawn and dusk.
evidence.observedEffect: Nesting was associated with a slight-to-major reduction in prey quantity and diversity compared with nonnesting fish.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Gut contents by nesting state and time of day
evidence.lifeStage: Adult parental males and nonnesting adults
evidence.novaApplicability: Direct feeding endpoint; transfer limited by sex, state, and single system
evidence.limitations: Defensive strikes may still occur; reduced feeding does not equal zero catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Dawn versus dusk samples of nesting and nonnesting fish.
evidence.observedEffect: Benthic prey formed a greater dietary proportion at dawn than dusk, while nesting status altered total diet.
evidence.limitations: No hook-and-line endpoint and no full environmental light record.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: North Anna River; spawning began in late May after water exceeded 20 C.
evidence.observedEffect: Nests occurred in pool habitat with low current velocity below 0.10 m/s and depths above 0.5 m; degree-days helped explain nest density.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Nest timing, density, depth, and velocity
evidence.novaApplicability: High geographic relevance for location context
evidence.limitations: Habitat occupancy and nest density are not feeding or catchability.

evidence.variable: Fish Guide gear and regional management
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Pennsylvania river fisheries.
evidence.observedEffect: Management guidance documents intentional angling, distribution, and fishery context.
evidence.limitations: Not an experimental bite-predictor source.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Barometric pressure, fronts, wind, ordinary rain, cloud cover, and moon phase.
evidence.observedEffect: No qualifying species-specific study directly isolated these variables for feeding, foraging, or hook-and-line catchability.
evidence.novaApplicability: Directly relevant to excluding unsupported weights
evidence.limitations: Absence of evidence does not prove no effect; it does preclude a defensible production rule.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Bimonthly sampling from January 1972 through June 1973 in two Florida rivers.
evidence.observedEffect: Aquatic and terrestrial insects formed the bulk of the diet; feeding was opportunistic and reflected available prey.
evidence.populationLocation: Suwannee and Santa Fe rivers, Florida
evidence.novaApplicability: Mechanistically relevant but geographically warmer than NOVA
evidence.limitations: Diet composition is not a direct hourly catchability measure.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Florida river samples; prolonged warm-season spawning.
evidence.observedEffect: Spawning extended from spring into fall, with greatest activity in late spring and summer.
evidence.novaApplicability: Timing is not transferable as an exact NOVA calendar
evidence.limitations: Warm Florida climate and long season limit transfer.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: 481 tagged fish; 189 recaptures within 60 days.
evidence.observedEffect: Most fish showed moderate mobility, upstream movements predominated, and annual sport harvest was estimated near 14.7%.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Tag recaptures, movement direction, and harvest
evidence.novaApplicability: Regional stream context; movement is not feeding
evidence.limitations: Tag returns depend on reporting, effort, and access.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Thirty-six South Carolina Piedmont beaver ponds.
evidence.observedEffect: Food occurred in 96.6% of examined stomachs; aquatic insects dominated, with fish contributing substantial volume.
evidence.novaApplicability: Piedmont relevance, but pond habitat differs from NOVA rivers
evidence.limitations: Presence of food in stomachs does not establish environmental bite multipliers.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Beaver ponds; water reached approximately 23 C during the spawning period.
evidence.observedEffect: Spawning occurred mainly May-August after water warmed to the reported level.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Gonadal condition, nests, and water temperature
evidence.novaApplicability: Context only; exact threshold is population- and habitat-specific
evidence.limitations: Do not convert a spawning observation into a feeding optimum.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Three lower-Piedmont streams spanning forested, suburban, and urban land cover.
evidence.observedEffect: Chironomids were major prey; fish shifted toward terrestrial prey where aquatic prey were less available.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Stomach contents, prey availability, growth, and stable isotopes
evidence.novaApplicability: Moderate regional transfer for prey context
evidence.limitations: Only three streams and limited sample sizes; land cover bundles multiple mechanisms.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Nine Georgia rivers; April-June flow metrics compared with annual growth.
evidence.observedEffect: Higher or more variable spring flow was associated with greater growth in most rivers; reported wet-year growth increments exceeded dry-year increments by age.
evidence.limitations: Growth is not feeding rate or catchability; correlations may reflect productivity and habitat.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Edisto River cohorts spanning drought and flood years.
evidence.observedEffect: A drought cohort dominated recruitment, and some growth intervals were greater during drought than flood conditions.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Age structure, cohort strength, and growth
evidence.novaApplicability: Useful contradiction to generic flood-benefit rules
evidence.limitations: Recruitment and growth are not short-term bite endpoints.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Virginia rivers, streams, and reservoirs.
evidence.observedEffect: Rock bass are an established and intentionally targeted Mid-Atlantic sportfish, especially in flowing waters.
evidence.limitations: Not a direct environmental bite function.

evidence.variable: Angler catch in the New River
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Standardized creel/angler-catch work in Virginia and West Virginia.
evidence.observedEffect: Rock bass were among the commonly caught species, confirming practical targetability in a regional river fishery.
evidence.populationLocation: New River, Virginia and West Virginia
evidence.limitations: Species catch proportion is confounded by abundance, gear, effort, and retention.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Yearling rock bass and pumpkinseed in Lake St. Clair macrophyte habitats.
evidence.observedEffect: Submersed vegetation altered habitat and food partitioning between the species.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Diet and habitat use across macrophyte conditions
evidence.limitations: Yearling stage and Great Lakes vegetation limit transfer; not hook-and-line catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Comparative tests of male centrarchid nest defense.
evidence.observedEffect: Rock bass males showed relatively short attack distance and among the lower attack probabilities in the compared species.
evidence.novaApplicability: Supports rejecting a generic spawning aggression bonus
evidence.limitations: Nest-defense tests are not feeding and may not resemble angling lures.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Adult natural-water feeding or standardized catchability across temperatures.
evidence.observedEffect: No qualifying portable temperature-response curve was identified.
evidence.novaApplicability: Direct reason to withhold a temperature rule
evidence.limitations: Growth, spawning, and habitat temperatures cannot substitute for feeding.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Species-specific feeding or angling response in mg/L or saturation.
evidence.observedEffect: No qualifying direct rock-bass feeding/catchability oxygen threshold was identified.
evidence.limitations: Habitat tolerance is not bite probability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Barometric pressure, fronts, wind, rainfall, cloud cover, and moon phase.
evidence.observedEffect: No qualifying rock-bass study directly isolated these variables for feeding or hook-and-line catchability.
evidence.limitations: Retinal morphology is not evidence for solunar or cloud scoring.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Comparisons among yearlings, adults, lake populations, streams, and experimental channels.
evidence.observedEffect: Responses differed by prey, size, habitat, and study system, requiring explicit transfer limits.
evidence.limitations: This is a synthesis conclusion rather than an independent experiment.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Experimental stream channels with shallow 7-10 cm and deep 35-38 cm treatments.
evidence.observedEffect: Predation by adult rock bass was greater in deep treatment for fantail darters and two sizes of central stonerollers.
evidence.novaApplicability: Direct feeding endpoint but highly conditional
evidence.limitations: Only two depths, artificial channels, and specific prey; do not create a smooth depth curve.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Cover absent versus present crossed with depth.
evidence.observedEffect: Depth and cover effects varied by prey species; pumpkinseed prey did not show the same depth response as stream fishes.
evidence.limitations: Cannot generalize a single cover or depth bonus across prey communities.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Rock bass angled with different hook types.
evidence.observedEffect: Hook type affected capture efficiency and injury, supporting gear-specific Fish Guide guidance.
evidence.novaApplicability: Direct angling endpoint, but gear rather than environment
evidence.limitations: Does not support weather, temperature, or habitat scoring.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Summer samples from a Big South Fork stream.
evidence.observedEffect: Rock bass consumed aquatic insects, crayfish, and fish, with diet varying by size and availability.
evidence.limitations: Seasonal diet composition is not a daily catchability function.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Telemetry/tag observations in Lake Ontario and tributaries.
evidence.observedEffect: Rock bass movement and tributary use varied through time and habitat.
evidence.limitations: Movement is not feeding, and Great Lakes context differs from NOVA streams.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Lake Opinicon spawning season.
evidence.observedEffect: Adults moved inshore, densities increased, and males established shallow nest territories on coarse substrate.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Movement, nest density, depth, and substrate
evidence.limitations: Aggregation and territoriality do not demonstrate increased feeding.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Comparative retinal structure of rock bass and bluegill.
evidence.observedEffect: Retinal morphology was interpreted relative to feeding ecology and visual environment.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Retinal anatomy and inferred visual function
evidence.limitations: Morphology cannot be translated into a direct low-light or cloud multiplier.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Pennsylvania fisheries.
evidence.observedEffect: Management material documents deliberate recreational fishing and population management.
evidence.limitations: Catch trends combine effort, abundance, regulations, and access.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Kankakee River life-history sampling
evidence.observedEffect: Shorthead redhorse consumed a broad range of mainly benthic invertebrate prey categories; the study characterizes trophic mode but does not quantify an environmental feeding response.
evidence.limitations: Exact diet percentages were not promoted because the relevant original table/page was not independently reproduced during this run. Diet composition is not a bite multiplier.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Agency profile
evidence.observedEffect: The species is associated with shallow, swift water over clean sand or gravel.
evidence.limitations: Habitat presence is not catchability or feeding rate.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Broad targeted search
evidence.observedEffect: No qualifying experiment linked temperature, flow, oxygen, diel period, turbidity, prey level, weather, or angling pressure to shorthead-redhorse hook-and-line capture probability.
evidence.limitations: Absence of qualifying research is not proof the fish cannot be intentionally targeted.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Species size, benthic feeding ecology, and documented human use
evidence.observedEffect: Intentional rod-and-line targeting is plausible, but predictive evidence is too sparse for an environmental BiteMap score.

sourceLocator.section: Species profile plus reviewed primary literature

evidence.limitations: Niche targeting may be underrepresented in formal research.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Summer collections in four Iowa rivers
evidence.observedEffect: Shorthead and silver redhorse diets showed substantial overlap (Morisita index C=0.67), confirming benthic-resource overlap rather than an environmental feeding optimum.
evidence.whatWasMeasured: Stomach contents, diet overlap, gill-raker morphology
evidence.limitations: Multi-species Iowa study; overlap does not indicate feeding intensity or hook-and-line catchability.

evidence.observedEffect: Adults were observed spawning at 16 C in Big Rock Creek.
evidence.limitations: Single spawning event; reproductive activity was measured, not feeding or catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Eggs incubated at mean 15.6 C
evidence.observedEffect: Eggs hatched 8 days after fertilization; newly hatched larvae averaged 10.0 mm total length.
evidence.limitations: Early-life development and survival are not adult feeding or angling endpoints.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Early May to mid-June across three Great Lakes basin rivers
evidence.observedEffect: Shorthead and silver redhorse runs occurred earlier and at lower water temperatures than black and river redhorse runs.
evidence.limitations: Run timing is confounded with reproduction, river-specific temperatures, flows, and sampling; no feeding endpoint.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Species-specific peak migration temperatures used in swim/physiology tests
evidence.observedEffect: Shorthead redhorse exhibited higher maximum metabolic rate and faster swimming than the two comparison redhorse species.
evidence.limitations: Physiological capacity and fishway performance do not establish feeding motivation or catchability.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Fishway passage monitored across years
evidence.observedEffect: Passage success and passage duration varied among species and years, with temperature and flow considered as modulators.
evidence.limitations: Movement endpoint; no ingestion, attack, or hook-and-line outcome.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Populations separated by barriers in Great Lakes basin rivers
evidence.observedEffect: Species traits mediated genetic consequences of fragmentation in shorthead and river redhorse.
evidence.limitations: Connectivity and genetics are location/conservation context, not feeding.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Grand River population
evidence.observedEffect: Age, growth, and mortality were estimated for shorthead redhorse.
evidence.limitations: Growth and mortality cannot be converted to bite optima.

evidence.variable: Regional habitat, diet, and reproductive context
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Virginia coolwater streams and reservoirs; agency account reports spring spawning as water begins to exceed 60 F
evidence.observedEffect: Adults use oxygenated coolwater streams, rocky or gravel habitats, seasonal riffle-run-pool features, cover, and reservoirs with submerged structure; males build and defend nests.
evidence.limitations: Agency synthesis does not quantify feeding, angling catchability, temperature response curves, or waterbody-specific timing. The 60 F statement is a regional spawning cue, not a bite threshold.

evidence.variable: Current velocity, depth, substrate, and light
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Shallow Flat River pools in summer; preferred reduced currents generally below 15 cm/s and depths greater than 45 cm
evidence.observedEffect: When current velocity was experimentally increased, bass spent less time in the habitat, foraged less, and moved more. Sun-versus-shade manipulation did not alter habitat use.
evidence.novaApplicability: Moderate qualitative relevance to Northern Virginia streams; exact velocities and depths are not portable
evidence.limitations: Only the abstract was accessed. Habitat occupancy and foraging observations are not hook-and-line catchability. The light result concerns habitat use, not feeding under cloud cover.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Mark-recapture sampling by angling and boat electrofishing in the Broad River, South Carolina
evidence.observedEffect: Angling and electrofishing had different capture probabilities and size selectivity. No PIT-tagged fish was recaptured by angling two days after initial capture, which the authors discussed as possible short-term trap shyness.
evidence.novaApplicability: Useful caution for interpreting catch rates and possible pressure effects; magnitude is not transferable
evidence.limitations: The study estimated abundance, not environmental bite response. Non-recapture after two days cannot isolate learning from location, effort, lure, or detection effects and is insufficient for a pressure-scoring function.

evidence.variable: Thermal feeding and performance thresholds - synthesis quality
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: North American literature synthesis reporting mixed values for feeding, growth, movement, and tolerance
evidence.observedEffect: The synthesis compiles cold-feeding and preferred-temperature estimates, but the values derive from different populations, life stages, acclimation histories, and endpoints and do not establish a portable adult bite optimum.
evidence.populationLocation: North American studies synthesized for Canadian risk assessment
evidence.novaApplicability: Useful for identifying research gaps, not for a numerical Northern Virginia score
evidence.limitations: Secondary synthesis mixes feeding, growth, preference, survival, and early-life evidence. Exact temperature thresholds remain unavailable for direct bite scoring.

evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Literature synthesis discussing oxygen concentrations for normal activity, spawning, embryos, and larvae
evidence.observedEffect: The synthesis indicates that oxygen requirements vary by life stage and endpoint, but it does not provide direct adult feeding or angling-catchability functions suitable for Northern Virginia.
evidence.populationLocation: North American studies synthesized for Canadian risk assessment
evidence.limitations: Secondary synthesis; survival, reproduction, and normal activity cannot be converted into adult feeding or catchability thresholds. Numeric model values are intentionally left null.

evidence.variable: Seasonal water temperature and annual activity
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Year-round monitoring from August 2021 through August 2024 across Lake Ontario and two St. Lawrence River reaches
evidence.observedEffect: Daily activity was lowest in winter, increased rapidly during spring, peaked in early summer, and declined through late summer and fall; metabolic-rate estimates peaked in August. Winter activity remained low but nonzero.
evidence.populationLocation: Eastern Lake Ontario and St. Lawrence River
evidence.novaApplicability: Strong species relevance, but Great Lakes climate and habitat differ from Northern Virginia rivers and reservoirs

sourceLocator.section: Results - Annual activity modelling; Results - Metabolic rate; Discussion

evidence.limitations: Acceleration and modeled metabolic rate are not feeding rate or hook-and-line catchability. Population, habitat, and climate affected the timing and magnitude of activity.

evidence.variable: Time of day and underwater light
evidence.exactConditionOrRange: Season-specific diel models across lake and river habitats
